title: Critically acclaimed fantasy deckbuilding board game gets crowdfunder for reprint, robots
content:
Gudnak is a gorgeous, critically acclaimed fantasy board game that has you join one of a diverse roster of factions and battle for a slowly dying world. You'll build a 20-card deck from eight factions and hundreds of individual cards, then take it to battle with up to three other players. If that sounds like your cup of tea, then you'll be pleased to know that Gudnak is getting a reprint along with a fresh new expansion, courtesy of a fully funded crowdfunder.

The Gudnak: Reprint and Guilds of Zarruhk Expansion crowdfunder is due to wrap up on October 14. However, at the time of writing, there's still a window of opportunity for anyone who might want to get in on this curious card-driven board game. Though very much a self-contained experience, Gudnak is intended to be a response to Magic: The Gathering and other card games where scalping and expensive decks can overshadow otherwise enjoyable experiences.

Though not on our best board games list, Gudnak enjoys critical acclaim with an 8.5 rating on BoardGameGeek. The Guilds Expansion looks poised to build on this success, adding modular robot fighters with programmable actions and new additions for existing factions.

You can get your hands on the Core Set with a pledge of $49 (£37), while the Guilds Expansion is available for $39 (£29). Both will set you back $88 (£66), while the Complete Collection, which includes the Core Set and all four expansions, comes to $199 (£150). Those looking for a more luxurious purchase can commit to the Deluxe Collection, which includes everything in the Complete Collection, along with a fancy playmat and a storage box for $269 (£203).

There are also very high-end options available for big spenders. For instance, the Everything Bundle comes to $599 (£452) and includes five sets, two booster boxes, 800 faction sleeves, two playmats, the storage box, two deck boxes, a hardcover, and a plushie.

title: There's less than a day for you to get in on this $2 million fantasy board game crowdfunder
content:
Board game crowdfunders can be a tricky business; the sheer number of titles vying for your time, attention and cash could be likened to a bucket full of crabs, each ruthlessly competing to get to the top. While the topmost crabs might not be everyone's favorite, it's worth highlighting any cancrine aspirants that manage to distinguish themselves. Enter: Heroes of Might and Magic 3: The Board Game, a tabletop adaptation of a beloved fantasy strategy video game by the same name. The folks at Archon Studio have raised over €1.8 million ($2 million) in pledges for the project with just under a day to go, at the time of writing.

The Heroes of Might and Magic 3: The Board Game crowdfunder centers around three new expansions in what the developers are calling the "last chapter" for the game: the Factory, Bulwark, and Forge expansions.

The game offers an adventure-driven strategy experience rooted in a colorful, if generic, fantasy world. You and up to three other players will make your way across an adventure map, engaging in turn-based battles using gorgeous miniatures. Given that the crowdfunder is due to end on October 12, there's not much time left to back the project (even if the core game never made our best board games list).

Those looking to get all the new expansions can pledge at the All New Big Box Vol. 3 level for €119.00 ($133). This includes the three expansions as well as the Golden Stretch Goals (of which there are many). This pledge is also available in a variant with separate boxes for its constituent elements. Conversely, if you've not got a copy of the main game, you can go for the Basic Vol. 3 pledge which offers the Core Game, Tower Expansion, Golden Stretch Goals and Regular Stretch Goals for the same price.

Shaded variants of both of these pledges are also available for €149.00 ($167). These include shaded versions of the miniatures from all of the above sets. Those wanting every single Heroes of Might and Magic 3: The Board Game product can go for the All In Vol. 3 €459.00 ($514). This is available in four variants, which you can check out on the campaign page itself.

title: Dwarfen throngs and pre-painted 40k battlefields stand out in the latest Warhammer preview
content:
In the depths of the Mortal Realms, old war drums sound once more. The Khazalite Holds, a brand new Age of Sigmar faction, take center stage in the latest Warhammer preview. This signals that the new sculpts will be available for pre-order imminently, ushering in a heartening return to the old-school Dwarfen aesthetics of yore. However, those of a more grimdark persuasion are also in for a major new release: pre-painted terrain. The Battlefields: Armageddon set represents the first Games Workshop terrain set of its kind and offers a novel option for those looking to set up a 40k battlefield without the usual hassle.

That said, as much as the new pre-painted terrain marks a bold departure for Games Workshop, it's the new Age of Sigmar faction that enjoys the top spot in the latest Warhammer Community preview.

The Khazalite Holds Army set promises a self-contained army consisting of 10 Clanshields, three Gholems of Gazul, an Oathkeeper Cannon, and dwarfen hero Hjulda Drakkblud. The sculpts are gorgeous, harkening back to the old Dwarf armies of Warhammer Fantasy while boasting the dynamic poses and impressive detail for which the modern Age of Sigmar range is known. The Army Set, along with every other product featured in the preview, will be available for pre-order next weekend, most likely on October 17.

Meanwhile, in the grim darkness of the far future, the Battlefields: Armageddon set is also up for preview. Games Workshop's first-ever pre-painted battlefield. The kit includes all the pieces, boards, and terrain area footprints needed to play any of the missions from the Chapter Approved 2026-27 Mission Deck. It includes eight Large Manufactorum Ruins, eight Small Manufactorum Ruins, two Shock Arrays, two Capacitor Stacks, four Rockrete Barricades, two Generator Shrines, and four Galvanic Pylons. 

The latest preview also includes a stunning new Warhammer Day commemorative miniature and a new Black Library novel: Shadow of the Silver Wolf. The novel follows Stormcast Eternal Neave Blacktalon and her allies as they find themselves in the nightmare-wreathed city of Greybank.

title: This new MTG Commander from Darkhold Destiny can become massive, despite having a 0/0 statline
content:
Given that it was only revealed on Friday, we've only seen a small number of cards from the upcoming MTG Darkhold Destiny expansion. All the same, some of these new reveals seem pretty massive, quite literally in the case of Gargantos, the Endbringer, a card that can grow to incredible sizes, despite technically being a 0/0.

If you're unfamiliar with Gargantos, they are a giant eldritch squid monster from Marvel lore. They briefly cameoed in the MCU, pursuing America Chaves in 2022's Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. They've not got a tremendous amount of lore, or much of a character arc, but they're a sinister Lovecraftian squid that roams the cosmos causing chaos.

Gargantos is due to be printed in Darkhold Destiny's Commander release, as a green and black four drop 0/0 with deathtouch. To prevent it from dying immediately, Gargantos enters play with three +1/+1 counters, and then during each of your upkeep steps, the number of +1/+1 counters on Gargantos doubles. Gargantos's massive size and world shattering power are then reflected by its ability to deal damage to each of your opponents whenever it damages one of them.

There's a lot to work with here. Make sure to include lots of effects to pile additional +1/+1 counters onto Gargantos to take full advantage of its doubling ability. Making the Squid unblockable, or else granting it flying or trample, will also allow you to benefit as much as possible from the fact that it spreads the combat damage around to each of your opponents whenever its attacks get through.

Because of Gargantos's green/black colour identity, it won't be eligible to be included in any of Darkhold Destiny's Commander Decks. Given that the preview we've seen of it is full art, it seems likely that it may show up in a scene box or another supplementary product.

Are there any magical Marvel characters that you're hoping to see in Darkhold Destiny?  Let us know in the Wargamer Discord.

On the Internet at Large

Welcome back to Content We Liked! Wonderfully gross.

title: This Pikachu in a raincoat is now the second most expensive Pokémon card ever sold
content:
Back in February, Wargamer covered the most expensive Pokémon card sale of all time, Logan Paul's PSA 10 Pikachu Illustrator, which sold for $16 million dollars (£12 million pounds). On September 28th, another Pikachu card earned a silver medal, selling for around half as much at $8.4 million dollars (£6.3 million pounds). This time, Pikachu was kitted out in a raincoat, and carrying an umbrella rather than a quill pen.

The card, unofficially known as "raincoat Pikachu", is a promo from a 2015 contest related to the old 3DS game Pokémon Art Academy. Pokémon fans were invited to upload picture of Pikachu drawn in Art Academy to Miiverse (a Nintendo based social network for the 3DS and the Wii U). Six winners were chosen, and the artists who drew them received 100 copies of the promotional Pikachu bearing their illustration.

While, with only 100 copies out there, "Raincoat Pikachu" is an exceedingly rare Pokémon card this sale breaks with precedent in a number of ways. According to data on the Pokémon TCG price tracking website Price Charting, four PSA ten copies of this card have been sold before for prices ranging from $14,000 (£10,500) to $26,000 (£19,600). While 26 thousand bucks is certainly significantly higher than my typical card gaming budget, it's only about 3% of the $8.4 million dollars of this particular sale.

Additionally, each of the other most expensive Pokémon Card sales has been for classic cards from the 1990s. We've already mentioned Logan Paul's $16 million dollar Pikachu Illustrator, which originates from a contest held in 1997. Then there's Trophy Pikachu No. 1 and Trophy Pikachu No.3, which sold for $3 million dollars (£2.2 million pounds) and $1.7 million dollars (£1.29 million pounds) respectively and were tournament prizes distributed in 1997 and 1998. While Raincoat Pikachu is similar to these cards in that it's a cute picture of the series mascot, it has a much less storied history than its Millennial rivals, given that it's thoroughly Gen Alpha with a 2015 birthday.

If it's raining outside, you could grab an umbrella and a raincoat like Pikachu, or you could stay in by the warm fire and browse the Wargamer Discord server.

title: The sapphic sci-fi TTRPG inspired by Marathon embodies indie chaos
content:
Some would have you  believe that the digitization of Tabletop RPGs is a modern invention. However, they are mistaken. It's far earlier than that. Barely a year after the release of certain dungeon crawler in 1974, developers Gary Whisenhunt and Ray Wood developed The Game of Dungeons for the PLATO system in 1975. The relationship between technology and tabletop technology has always been strong. This indie TTRPG shows just how well the two can co-exist.

Also, it's queer as hell.

Have You Been A Good Girl, or HYBAGG for short, is a sci-fi TTRPG where two players take on the role of GIRLs, spiteful consciousness shoved into vessels under the thrall of a THRONE, a matriarchal AI that aims to dominate all others. One GIRL attacks. The other GIRL defends.  If you expected a straightforward game with analogues to DnD classes, this is definitely not that.

HYBAGG utilizes dice rolls and instant messages in its gameplay loop. The attacker rolls six times with a d66 to determine their KEYS, each number attached to a word they MUST use in their message. Similarly, the defender rolls seven times to determine their LOCKS. An attacker wins if they are able to utilize five of their six KEYS over the course of their messages.

A defender wins if they are able to bait the attacker into "tripping" three of their LOCKS in their messages. If the attacker trips the seventh LOCK in the list, however, it's an instant win for the defender. All of this encourages players to engage with roleplay aggressively. You bait each other with the wrong words to force self-realization, a verbal version of Battleship where each word is a sapphic stab to the gut.

There's obviously more to the mechanics, but that alone makes it one of the most fascinating duo experiences. The best couples board games ought to make the players feel closer, and this game is guaranteed to do that. The striking language and Marathon-inspired aesthetic  captures the chaotic atmosphere of a bleak sci-fi future.

The fear of saying the wrong things, the rage against an authority imposing its will upon your body, the catharsis of navigating language and coming out as yourself, the game explores queer themes in such an esoteric yet undeniably captivating manner. If you're at all interested in TTRPGs that take big swings in its design, this is a must-play.

Have You Been A Good Girl is available on itch.io.

title: The Star Wars DnD crossover needs to overhaul the 5.5e system
content:
When Wizards of the Coast announced an official crossover between Dungeons and Dragons and Star Wars, I was more cautious than excited. The publisher is all in on crossovers across all its properties, as Magic: The Gathering players can attest. As far as crossovers though, Star Wars is a property WoTC already has history with. In the 2000s, the publisher released D20 Star Wars, a system now iconic thanks to its adaptation in Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic.

But can modern WotC make Star Wars feel like Star Wars in DnD 5.5e?

On October 9, 2026, WotC revealed Star Wars: Tyro Squadron Adventures at New York Comic Con as a supplement to the upcoming D&D Star Wars Core Rules book. The publisher states it will follow a secret Rebel crew in a fight against the Empire, specifically set during the Original Trilogy.  These details, unfortunately, do little to answer my biggest concern with Star Wars in modern D&D: Force powers. While some DnD classes have options to emulate the Force, I'm a firm believer that the Force mustn't be treated the same way as spells.

The excellent Star Wars RPG from Fantasy Flight Games does a stellar job of adapting the Force with a modern rule set. However, I will focus on WotC's previous foray into the Force. In Star Wars: Saga Edition, the Force manifests in so much more than just spell slots. Every character, just as in the canon, can "use the Force", affecting their rolls via a pool of Force Points, which refresh at the GM's discretion.

For those who want the cooler Force powers, they must build towards it with feats, gaining access to even more powers and talent  with unique backgrounds, ala DnD races. Best of all, there was no need for a finite Short Rest after every encounter to refresh uses. Force users can simply meditate for one minute and regain all of their Force Powers, which keeps the pace free-flowing.

I say all this to paint a picture of how 5.5e as it stands cannot be the basis for Force powers. The rest system and spell slots are limiting for the stories that Star Wars tells, particularly with the generous use of Force powers. The Fighter subclass Psi Warrior, DnD's attempt at a Jedi Knight, is severely underpowered in 5.5e, especially compared to Battle Master and Echo Knight. Force powers need to feel cool and accessible every encounter, and they must be more than just a spell to cast every nap.

I recently covered the DnD versions of WoW classes, and even for a franchise that is inspired by Dungeons and Dragons, WotC didn't quite capture the energy of its collaborator. WotC certainly doesn't need to rehash anything they've done from a decade ago, but I hope they learned lessons from it. There's not much detail on what the D&D Star Wars Core Rules will contain in 2027, but hopefully, it does more than just repaint 5.5e in Star Wars colors.

While you wait Star Wars D&D to come out, why not discuss its place in the TTRPG landscape with other tabletop fans over at the Wargamer Discord?

title: They're actually letting Space Marines be sneaky in the upcoming 40k RTS
content:
To the uninitiated, Space Marines can often seem monolithic and samey - a superpowered gruel smothered in Leadbelcher paint. However, take even a moment to look into their lore, and you'll find a kaleidoscope of colour - something that upcoming 40k RTS video game Dawn of War 4 seems to understand, if its most recent preview trailer is any indication. Due to release on December 3, Dawn of War 4 intends to bring four factions to your computer screen: Orks, Necrons, Adeptus Mechanicus and, as exhibited in the gorgeous new faction trailer, the Space Marines themselves.

Dropped on the official 40k YouTube channel, the Space Marines Faction trailer places the Dark Angels and the Blood Ravens front and center. The trailer assures us that both chapters will be able to play to their strengths, with the Blood Ravens being scouty and sneaky while the Dark Angels trample their foes with overwhelming, direct force. Their leaders reflect this, with the Blood Ravens being led by either a master scout or a chief librarian (read: powerful space wizard) while the Dark Angels follow either a Captain clad in Terminator Armor or a Chaplain on a bike. 

The trailer then gives us an overview of the different units available to the 40k faction. As well as the typical mainstay of Intercessors, Assault Intercessors and Infiltrators, we're also getting Outriders - noteworthy since bikers have been absent in every previous Dawn of War title. It's gratifying to see the heavier Primaris-era options finally get represented in the series. The Bladeguard Veterans look gorgeous, especially with their glowing Storm Shields and big, sweepy combat animations. 

Drop pods offer an opportunity for the rapid deployment of reserves alongside other orbital elements, including strikes and the ability to flat-out call down buildings from space. This is gratifying news if you, like me, miss the large-scale base building of the first Dawn of War game.

title: Detachment Focus: Butchers of Khorne
content:
In this series of articles we take a deep dive into a specific Detachment for a faction, covering the faction’s rules and upgrades and talking about how to build around that faction for competitive play. In this article, we’re covering the Butchers of Khorne Detachment for World Eaters.

Introduced with the initial deluge of 11th edition Detachments, the Butchers of Khorne helped fill a gap World Eaters fans had long been grousing over: The lack of support for the faction's Terminators. It doesn't finally give us a character to lead them, but it does make them substantially better, giving the army a way to make good use of its elite infantry.

Detachment Overview

Disposition: Take and Hold

Detachment Cost: 1 DP

The Butchers of Khorne Detachment is all about your Terminators, finally giving World Eaters players a way to represent the faction's deadliest elite murderers on the table. There are two very good enhancement options here, one of which lets you essentially build the army to the Take and Hold Disposition the Detachment offers. The recent changes to the Berzerker Warband Detachment and marine stats have also made this Detachment more valuable - you have better options to run alongside your Terminators, more ways to buff them, and they're tougher - if a bit more expensive - on the table.

Detachment Rule: Wrath of Khorne

At the start of the Fight phase, if a friendly Terminator Squad is engaged, you can make a Blessings of Khorne roll and activate a blessing. That blessing is active for all your friendly Terminator squads in addition to any others you have active until the end of the phase.

This is really great - it gives you a ton of utility, and can be activated separately for each of your terminator units, and twice per round if you're stuck in combat the entire time. The downside is the randomness - it can be a bit too easy to whiff on your rolls when you need something good, but you're more or less guaranteed to get Rage-Fuelled Invigoration (6" Consolidate move) all the time, so it's unlikely you'll ever end up with nothing.

Because this activates at the start of the Fight phase, you can essentially prioritize movement tricks with your first roll and then use your extra blessing roll to snag a fight buff later. It's also great for activating Total Carnage (4+ fight on death) when you're charged or about to fight - that's not necessarily something you want to activate at the start of the battle round but is great to have in a pinch when you're charged by something particularly nasty. Likewise, the aforementioned Rage-Fuelled Invigoration is rarely something you want to actually spend a blessing on at the start of a round if you have other options, and it's near-guaranteed as a pull here. This ability is also great for getting a second shot at something like Lethal or Sustained Hits, if you had to spend one of your two blessings on +1 to charges.

This also plays much better with Angron, whose resurrection ability eats your Blessings for a turn. Now you can Resurrect the angry primarch and still activate a blessing for each of your terminator units in combat when they fight.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Enhancements

Both of these are for Terminator squads only.

  • Sanctified in Slaughter (Upgrade, 15 pts): This unit gets +1 OC. This is fine, and helps with the fact all your Terminators are OC1. It's a good bonus to have if you're planning on playing Take and Hold with units of 10 Terminators, as being OC 1 can make it easy for you to have objectives stolen out from under you. However chances are good you just don't take this because your alternative is Gore-Stained Veterans.
  • Gore-Stained Veterans (Upgrade, 20 pts): This unit’s melee attacks get +1 WS. Stepping up to hitting on 2s is a decent improvement in your reliability, and this combos extremely well with both the +1 Attack from Berzerker Warband and Angron's new aura ability to re-roll 1s to hit and wound.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Stratagems

All three of the Stratagems on offer here can only be used on Terminator Squads. They're good effects, and priced to move. Wrath Beyond Reason will cost you 2 CP, which is pretty common for -1 damage effects.

  • Focused Ferocity (1 CP) - used in the Fight phase when a Terminator squad is selected to fight. That unit gets +1 attacks for its melee weapons. Straightforwardly good, and really nasty when combined with the +1 Attack from Berzerker Warband. Having 5A on your power fists is insanely good value, or if you're trying to go all-out against hordes, 7 on your paired accursed weapons.
  • A Trophy for the Throne (1 CP) - used in the Fight phase when a Terminator squad is selected to fight. That unit gets +1 to wound against MONSTER or VEHICLE units. Great for adding some oomph to your otherwise middling-strength stuff punch through heavier units. You more or less need this for your power fists to get there against heavier targets, and combining +1 to wound with LETHAL HITS and re-rolling 1s with Angron really smooths out the curve on your Terminators.
  • Wrath Beyond Reason (2 CP) - Used in your opponent’s Shooting phase when an enemy unit’s attacks target a Terminator squad. Those ranged attacks have -1 Damage for this activation. Great for keeping your Terminators protected, especially if someone is dropping damage 3 shots on them. Between this and the melee version in Berzerker Warband, you have a solid way to keep your Terminators on the table longer regardless of your opponent's army.

Note that because they’re both in the Fight phase, there’s no way to double up on Focused Ferocity and A Trophy for the Throne - you’ll be getting one or the other.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Playing This Detachment

If you're running Butchers, you're running Terminators, no two ways about it. Prior to the September Dataslate, Butchers armies tended to be strong teams lists, typically running two 10-man units of Terminators with the Gore-Stained Veterans upgrade to give them a ton of killing power in the middle of the table. Faster movement combined with the extra buffs and attacks really make them a nasty unit for board control, able to really surprise opponents in a pinch. Those armies tended to run Butchers + Vessels + Brazen Engines, as those were kind of the only real options if you wanted to run the army.

However the September balance update threw a big curveball, radically changing how armies build around Butchers. First, it made those terminators T6 - a huge improvement. Second, it made them more expensive. But third and most importantly, it made Berzerker Warband a 2 DP Detachment. This now means that you can take Butchers and Warband, giving you access to +1 Attack all the time, extra AP on the charge, -1 damage in melee, and the Purge the Foe Disposition. Take and Hold is still a fine play for Butchers, but the added damage output options really make the prospect of those terminator bricks much more compelling.

Previously, lists ran Butchers + Vessels, an odd fit given Terminators have no leader option in the book. Being able to take Butchers + Warband opens things up considerably, though you'll likely still want a Daemon Prince on hand to make your Command Points go further - and to pop -1 damage in melee. Beyond that, Take and Hold lists for Butchers tend to run two units of ten with the Gore-Stained Veterans upgrade, opting for raw power and damage output over OC. Of course, you still can run a list with Vessels and Brazen Engines, and that's just fine if you also want to bring lots of Daemon Princes and a Defiler. Though if you go the Warband route, Angron may make more sense than a Defiler as your big threat, given his new aura makes the Terminators better and he's able to show up again later without completely destroying your ability to get Blessings in combat.

Strengths

  • Terminators. The buffs your Terminators get here are great, and being able to upgrade a unit with +1 WS or +1 OC is a big deal. If you want to run Terminators, you need to be running this Detachment.
  • Versatility. Choosing a benefit for each unit when the Fight phase rolls around (based on what you roll, anyways), gives you quite a few options and the ability to chase the dream of having all three melee buffs active at once.

Weaknesses

  • Variable Detachment Benefit. Getting an extra Blessing of Khorne roll is great... until you completely whiff on the roll when you need a specific benefit.

Final Thoughts

As we move into the new, T5 Marine meta, expect Butchers to have play for World Eaters, especially when combined with Berzerker Warband. That +1 Attack does a ton of work and while S5 Accursed Weapons may not be as good as they used to be, having T6 Terminators should help keep them on the table longer, particularly as you have -1 Damage stratagems to deal with your nastiest threats.

title: Roundtable: Codex Adeptus Custodes (11th Edition)
content:
Our review of the 11th Edition Codex: Adeptus Custodes dropped last weekend and the new book has sparked a ton of conversation among our 40k authors about the new faction, their direction, and how they’ll play. We sat the crew down to talk about the new book, offer their thoughts, and talk about what they like, don’t like, and how they see the army in the meta shaping up as we head into the end of the year.

THE ROUNDTABLE

  • Robert “TheChirurgeon” Jones
  • Struan “Struj” Robertson
  • Jag the Power Armor Enthusiast
  • Liam “Corrode” Royle
  • Isaac Terada

What’s your overall impression of the new book?

TheChirurgeon: I honestly like the new book. I think philosophically it makes a lot more sense for how the Adeptus Custodes should feel on the tabletop - a very small number of incredibly elite soldiers who can take on any threat in the galaxy. The Ork and Space Marine codexes both felt fairly generic and directionless to me, and while some of that is likely to be a result of those being armies with too many units, there’s clearly an idea behind what Custodes are supposed to be, and that makes for a stronger book overall. The rules here are good, they make you want to play the army, and they communicate what the force is all about -  and that’s what should happen when you pick up a codex.

Jag The Power Armor Enthusiast: The book does an amazing job of giving Custodes a badly needed wider toolbox with almost flawless internal balance to the Custodes themselves. There are more “optimal” takes on the whole. But you can take almost anything in this book and be competitively viable, that is worthy of high praise especially in comparison to the last book that had been kept together with duct tape and prayers of hope to the Emperor on his Throne. This Codex should be the gold standard for future codexes as it does not single out only one type of model in any case, but focuses on tight groupings of models. Thrilling to behold! There are small issues. But I can see these being handled in a dataslate update with a little luck. 

Struan: I think it’s great. As a competitive player first, a reluctant painter second and a lore enthusiast some way behind in 3rd, this book has me reading up on the Auramite clad Demigods conducting Blood Games… What have I become? The detachments feel thematic and do the things that the Shield Hosts are supposed to do and the models feel strong like they’re supposed to. None of this “Space-Marine-Terminator with +1T” from 10th Edition. I don’t think it’s perfect, but I think it’s a very promising sign of future 11th Edition codices.

Liam: To me, the 11th edition codexes so far show a similar philosophy of re-imagining factions, getting down to the very fundamentals of what a model is meant to represent. I disagree with Rob that Orks and Space Marines were directionless; I think they have a very clear direction along these lines. If you want to make Orks have meaningful shooting, why insist on it hitting on 5s, just because that’s how it was 30 years ago? Why must a Space Marine be T4? Why are boltguns a standing joke instead of a terrifying volley of explosive shells? The Custodes codex takes this re-imagining and runs with it, turning your Custodians into the true battlefield demi-gods the fluff would like them to be. Just a few years ago people were turning up with lists with bricks of 10 Custodians in them, quickly cut down to 5 - but then you just ran twice as many. At the end of 10th edition you’d see 6 units of the things inside of three Land Raiders - a model count not meaningfully different than any other power armour faction. Now the maximum you have in any unit is 4 models, including a character, and they’re all hard as nails and hit like trains. If you really want to spam you can run nothing but basic Custodian infantry and attached characters, giving a total model count of about 21 and room for very little else. It makes them feel genuinely elite; each dead guy is meaningful because it’s 25%-33% of your unit’s total strength.

TheChirurgeon: It’s not that I think having shooty Orks or T5 marines is a problem - though it’s funny and weird that almost nothing is T4 now - but that these books have armies which can just do everything and so feel much less focused. If Orks have good shooting, fast vehicles, good melee, and T5, what are they actually bad at? It’s not that Orks can have good shooting or that it has to be BS 5+; it’s that they have to be bad at something. That’s how good design works. 

In that regard, Custodes have an even clearer identity this time around, and I think that’s just easier when you have fewer units in an army - makes internal balance easier when you can give everything a defined role.

Isaac: Overall I think the changes made to this book are night and day to the 10th version of Custodes. Do I think it is perfect? No, there are some issues with the codex overall but I think this is a third codex that has really shown what GW is looking at when trying to design 11th codexes with the detachment point systems in mind. Looking inside the codex, these new detachments, the templating of abilities, the updated datasheets, all of it comes together to really make me, a player who never really saw an interest in Custodes, want to play them, which I think is exactly what you want from a codex revamping a faction from the ground up. 

What does the new book get right?

Struan: Detachment Balance. There doesn’t appear to be a “correct” way to take the army and its list-building. I think that’s a huge win for fans of Adeptus Custodes. Some detachments are looking more powerful than others initially, which is only natural, but I’m yet to see anything stand out head-and-shoulders as the objectively strongest way to do it. Mixing and matching detachment options is actually interesting with really tough trade-offs to “grab the good stuff”.

Jag: Almost everything is awesome in this book, gone are the days of Triple Wardens and Blade Champions, Gold Horde and Draxus as the must haves. Whoever wrote this should get a raise in that regard. Every Custodian option has a role, it's no longer “Well, maybe you run Axes if X-Y-Z line up.” No, you can run a highlander list of every option and be a genuine terror to behold. Also, allowing Trajann to join Terminators is one of the smartest choices, more named Characters should be able to jump in and attach to different unit types, do more with this GW, people will love it! Every detachment combination is at least in theory a frightening sight at its best combination, or good under the right meta at worst. That's a feat of good writing when I can assemble my Shadowkeepers fluff list and operate on the assumption that when I face a melee heavy assault, I am ready for it. But if I go to a tournament, I can still switch in for Dread Host with Lions and Morotoi. This is a badly needed injection of flavor to the game, and I hope this is the design ethos for future codexes with regards to balancing flavor and balance competitively. I am excited to play Custodes for the first time in years, and I praise Games Workshop's writers for doing so. The expectation bar had fallen through the basement and into the foundation, these writers not only met the bare minimum, they surpassed it in almost perfect form.

Struan: Hear-hear. Liam: Flicking through this book for the first time was genuinely exciting. Everything looked cool, everything had big and meaningful changes. Integrating the units from 30k into the baseline codex was a great choice. The detachments have strong, meaningful direction and purposeful design that I think is missing a bit from Space Marines. I think you can make a case for any of the Shield Hosts, and the rest all work for their intended purpose really nicely - whatever direction you want to take your list in, there’s something to suit. As you probably already guessed, I’m a big fan of the way that all the dials have been turned up on the datasheets to make the units much more elite-feeling.

TheChirurgeon: The first impression of this book was definitely eye-popping - and I think that’s a good thing. You want someone reading a book to be excited about the rules and the possibilities of what units can do - that’s good design and good marketing. ANd I think they nailed it in that regard. The points also feel solid; once I saw them I felt better about the datasheets.

What does the new book get wrong?

TheChirurgeon: I really wish the Shield Host Detachments were 2 DP (with some added stratagems/enhancements to match). This is part of an ongoing problem I have with 11th edition Detachment philosophy generally, where I think the most common way to build should be to take a 2 DP + a 1 DP detachment. This has the added benefit of not needing any of the SHIELD HOST tags; if they’re all 2 DP then they’re already mutually exclusive. 

Struan: The naming of the infantry variants. Sentinel Guard Sodality and Custodian Guard Sodality… shorthanding these guys is a nightmare! ‘Sentinel’ and ‘Custodian’ is out because the army are all Custodians… ‘Guard’ and ‘Guard, well that’s self-explanatory and the same can be said for ‘Sodality’. Shield Boys/Girls and Spear Boys/Girls it is… until people see your Wardens with spears… FML.

Jag: Why, and I must ask this. WHY were Sisters of Silence, so badly, badly shafted this round? There is so much more that can be done here with Sisters of Silence! Why not have their ability interact when in proximity to a Psyker trying to use their abilities? I'm not saying they should uninteractively shut OFF Psychic powers, no. That's going too far. But have their fluff of being a walking psychic 5G Dead Zone cause other problems? Like say “On a 1/2/3 when casting, your power causes the unit to battleshock” make it so facing the Sisters is a legitimate threat to Psykers in more than just a Feel No Pain to Psychic attacks and an Aura that boosts the Aegis ability. Yes it's incredibly funny when one single Sister of Silence no sells Magnus, but it's not funny for the player controlling Magnus. Have Sisters do more, especially when Sisters of Silence are now a single box with Aleya being sent to Legends and reducing the model count even further. It's such a kick to the gut for the fans of Sisters of Silence and the faction is clinging to hope for more models, more support, anything. My only other major complaints with the datasheets is the weird shafting of the Venatari that are packing pistols and buckler, I get the idea behind it, but for a unit with so little offensive power? I'd hope for a buff to their shooting, or at the very least, a points drop, especially when the Ka'Tah enhancements render the need for a generic action performer unit much lower than before for Custodes. Also, why is the Coronus allowing disembark and shoot? The Special Spears are legends, and Terminators can deep strike, so… what's the point of this? Let it have Assault Ramp, if you're worried about the return of Triple Land Raiders and Golden Horde style plays, no, it's really hard to do that now GW. 

I also second The Chirugeon's complaints regarding Shield Host, this focus on a ton of 1DPs while fun to try and build around, limits fluff and design space in my view as we have mostly just “well X unit gets Y ability” cool, but how about some zones of control, or synchronized auras? Looping back to the Sisters Discussion, Talons of the Emperor was a shining diamond in the otherwise festering disaster of the 10th edition book and I hope at some point it's added back as a 2DP, it was fun, it made Sisters better, while offering a unique style to Custodes that rewarded synergy, this Codex has small bits of that, but this is where I wished the Codex had experimented more with. I think this is where the Chapter Specific Detachments from the Space Marine Codex can feed into ideas for subfaction detachments in the future. Still, as lengthy as my remarks are, it's a comparative small complaint in comparison to the wide successes of this Codex. 

TheChirurgeon: As a Thousand Sons player, I’m fine never seeing Sisters of Silence on the table again. But also, they just brought back the goddamn army-wide Feel No Pain for Custodes against mortals so they’re a pain in the ass even without Sisters on the table. I'm just generally not a fan of anti-psyker rules in the game as they tend to disproportionately punish 2-3 armies and do nothing against another third.

Liam: I just don’t have it in me to care that much about Sisters of Silence as they currently exist. They’re not interesting or exciting at all, they’re cheap filler to allow you to run a handful of units for mission play when sending 200pts of Custodians to do it would be excessive. It’s like getting upset about lack of Gretchin support in Orks - there’s just not enough meat on those bones for it to ever be a viable playstyle, so if you were expecting more you were only setting yourself up for disappointment. SoS getting the significant range expansion that one 30k book suggested might happen would be cool and turn them into a real faction, but for now, whatever.

Otherwise, I don’t think there’s many misses in this book really. The Aquilons with solarite gauntlets maybe struggle a little for a role, as do the gun and shield Venatari. The sword and board Shield-Captain is so wildly better than the other versions that you wonder a little why the other choices exist. I typically agree with Rob that 2 + 1 is a better design approach for detachments than 1 + 1 + 1, but I think it actually works here; you basically pick a Shield Host, then pick two types of units to buff, in an army where you probably only have two types of units because of how few of them you can take. That works for me, philosophically. I think the Shield Host approach is also helpful because it has the anchor of being themed around existing sub-factions, which is what was missing from Space Marines and Orks, and it creates a sensible reason for them to be UNIQUE.

TheChirurgeon: I think Sisters could be a viable army with a little work, but I don’t think they should be - they’d be massively overtuned against Grey Knights and Thousand Sons and undertuned against everything else. It’s kind of like the Grey Knights/Deathwatch problem, where they serve much better as an add-on unit or small force than a full army. And while I like them and want them in the army, I also think that pure Custodes armies should be viable. If you can’t run an army entire of golden armor walking tanks, what are we doing here? 

Struan: Chipping back in with a slightly more sensible gripe than naming conventions, I agree with Jag and Liam that the Pistol Venatari are a little lacking and I think they’ll struggle to get on the table at a non-narrative game. But come on guys: Witchseekers are very real into a whole host of targets. That flamer is no joke. And a 7” move unit with 7” scout with assault flamers is always going to be at least OK. AND they are pretty aggressively costed in comparison to the rest of the units.

TheChirurgeon: Yeah the turn 1 Movement on the Witchseekers is like the first thing I noticed in the book once I saw that Land Raiders were gone - “Who is the Shock Assault rule for?” I asked, as I whipped through the pages. Then I saw the Witchseekers and went “ooooooh.” Yeah the flamers aren’t Rubrics good but they’ll do just fine.

Honestly the biggest problem with the new book is that it’s good - our negative review of the bad Codex did way more page views and generated a ton more discussion. No one actually wants to be happy.

How did GW do with the points?

Note: The final points aren’t yet confirmed, but we expect few changes between now and the release.

Struan: I think they did a great job. I think they are objectively overcosted, especially on the infantry. As someone playing in the competitive sphere I think it’s totally correct to go too high than too low on release. I am sad as someone looking to play as the Adeptus Custodes, but I am so so grateful as someone that might need to play into the Golden Horde.

TheChirurgeon: I think everyone on our team who looked at the rules for Custodes before points spent the first ten minutes going “oh wow this is bullshit,” followed by an exasperated “well, we’ll see what the points look like.” When the points finally did show up, I think they got them about perfect. I agree that Terminators and non-terminator infantry might be a bit too close in cost, but I don’t think Custodians and Wardens can go any lower.

That said, having really high point costs on models makes balancing very difficult - when your cheapest models are 80 points, shifting a list’s point costs by 10-20 points makes no difference. And the difference between two and three units of Wardens is massive - large enough that it will be difficult to make small tweaks to the army.

Liam: Yeah, the first impressions of this book were that it would be wildly powerful, and then when we saw the points and realised they had actually gone as extreme on “very elite but very pricy” as it looked like it ought to be we breathed a sigh of collective relief. Don’t get me wrong, these guys are good, but for my first go at putting a list together I wrote down what I thought was a pretty conservative, low-unit-count army and when I added it up it came out to 2,470pts. I can definitely see a world where the army gets caught in a trap a bit like the one big Knights have - 4 is too few, 5 is too many - and it’s a struggle to make meaningful balance changes via points, but at the moment I think they’re in a good place and we can worry about that down the line.

Jag: Echoing the sentiments here, there's some real rough decisions made here with things like Dreadnoughts being a cheaper take than the infantry. Especially Wardens. Yes, always active AoC is powerful and will make a lot of armies packing majority AP-1 weapons beyond frustrated, but the dreaded and hated 4+ FNP is gone GW, you can let the points come down. I should not have to pay more than a Grav-Tank for 3 infantry bodies who will drop dead to a few good swings of a Thunder Hammer. 

How do you think the army will play? What will successful lists look like?

TheChirurgeon: One of the most interesting shifts here is that while Custodes generally got deadlier by model, the infantry kind of got less deadly by unit. Yeah, you do more damage with your spears and axes, but you don’t have as many shots or attacks as you did before when you were running units of 6. So you have this interesting push-and-pull where Custodes got way more durable, but are on the whole less deadly with their infantry - when I look at Allarus Terminators with Axes, my thoughts are “wow 4 damage” followed by “oh but only 3 attacks, who cares?”

Where things did get deadlier though, is vehicles - those are so nasty here, and Dreadnought lists are going to be a nightmare.

Jag: This I think is going to test a long held belief of mine. Namely that GW has historically overvalued Wounds and toughness. Marines going to T5/6, and Custodes going to T7/8 is impressive on paper and has triggered sentiments of “Custodes are basically War Dogs now!” The reality is way less obvious. If I have a squad of 3 Custodian Guard get attacked by 10 Thunder Hammer and Stormshield Terminators? They are not going to last when in the face of copious amounts of 2D/3D/D3+2/D6+DIE weapons. In a vacuum, T7 5W a model is nasty, but when I lose 2 of my 3 Custodian Guards, the swing back is way *less* intimidating, especially when SH/LH army wide in melee is gone (except for Shield Host). And to be clear, I welcome that change, SH+LH has been a crutch of too many armies for too long. If anything, we can soon see a change with Custodes if things get too bad by changing squad sizes. We've seen GW make that change in the past and with good results. I think this means a lot of lists will be focused on Dreadnoughts with light infantry support, and I fully believe that a mechanized Custodes force of Caladius tanks, Pallas shoot and scoot, Dreadnought frontliners and the bare minimum of infantry are going to be pants browning monsters to deal with for a lot of armies. Could be wrong, but when the choice is a Contemptor or a squad of Guard? You go with the Contemptor a lot of the time. Not always, but it's hard to turn down an even faster and more destructive killing machine. 

Struan: I agree with the above points. The jump to S8 on the classic Guardian Spear doesn’t really move the dial on lethality. When compared to our S7 in 10th Edition you’re still going to wound elves & Guardsmen on 2s and you’re still going to wound Marines and Terminators on 3s. One more attack doesn’t help when you have 2 or 3 fewer guys.

Meltas are a big problem with the flattening of their damage. 6W models really, really hate new melta profiles where every failed save is 80-100 points removed from the board.

All that said, I think we’re likely to see builds with Characters and Dreads early on. People are going to roll out a very expensive Warden squad into a few different profiles and go “that’s it?” and want to nuke things. You know what nukes things? Dual Caestus Fists baby.

Jag: Make sure you play Pacific Rim music when your Telemon is punching a Norn to death. Liam: The possibility not mentioned here is massed jetbikes, which are both tougher (Gyrfalcons substantially so) and faster than anything else. That feels like an avenue at least worth exploring.

Otherwise yeah, the lists I’ve run so far have been one of each Dreadnought with some infantry support, and that felt great.

It seems like once the book releases we’ll have that meta for the rest of the year. How do you think Custodes will fit into that meta?

Jag: We've seen a few test games where new SM and Orks have not liked facing Custodes. Yet that's not a good barometer in my opinion. There's a clear divide with 11E Codexes and 10E Codexes and Supplements. With the newer codexes, rerolls have been heavily reigned in, LH+SH are conditional (mostly), and there's a concerted effort to try and make these armies match their fluff even if it does not always meet the mark. Try putting a squad of Custodians up against Drukhari who will laugh their asses off at this thing called “Toughness” and instead Anti-Infantry the Golden Bananas off the board, or Howling Banshees who will throw enough 2D Anti-Infantry swings to give Custodian Guard pause. Or just throw Rogal Dorns at your opponent, or Riptides, hell! Flawless Blades in Emperor's Children are looking damn scary with their way of basically playing AoS and ignoring Toughness values. This codex and army looks intimidating on paper. But remember that 11E has skewed towards shooting heavily. Custodes are still at their core a melee army. They're a lot faster, they're kinda tougher, but this edition is ramping UP the lethality. When we see 4D weapons on Axes and Trajann that is… concerning. To say the least. So, are we headed for a power armor meta? Maybe. I love my power armor, I love watching everyone fight it out in melee. But I don't think the doomsayers are quite accurate. We shall see. 

Struan: Weirdly, I can’t see it changing things very much. Custodes as an army to play as and against will change dramatically but it does very much feel middle of the pack (at least initially!). With the new toolbox available, I think strong players will commit some atrocities, but I think weaker players will really struggle. The first time someone overextends their hyper-elite army into a gunline and loses 70% of them, those golden lads and ladettes will be placed gently back on shelves. Either way, I’m excited to play more with them and test out the genuinely varied options available.

Liam: I think it ends up in a similar place to where Knights often do, as an army with a good but unspectacular win rate, the ability to gatekeep poor players off the top tables, but maybe not quite enough oomph to reliably take down a whole event. And, much like Knights, it’ll divide opinions. Bad players playing against Custodes will feel like it’s oppressive, as their opponent no-sells all their offence, seems to have the right kind of karate for any situation, and deals out high-quality attacks all over the place. Bad players with Custodes will overextend themselves and get their small, valuable units killed for no benefit. It’ll be very difficult for Custodes armies to bring meaningful screening except maybe running a bunch of Witchseekers to push out early with Scouts, which makes them vulnerable to other armies with deep strike/Rapid Ingress threats. It’ll be interesting to see where an experiment like this lands and whether the design team are able to keep it working throughout the edition.

TheChirurgeon: Bad players with Custodes are always such a dangerous prospect. Yeah they overextend and try and do too much but did you count on them just passing a bunch of 4+ saves and no-selling your damage, idiot? You did not, and now that Shield Captain is taking a dump on your home objective. 

Ultimately I think Custodes have a playstyle that’s focused more on durability and holding objectives than pure offense, and that’s a problem in 11th edition, where even the most durable units can just get wiped off the table by land speeders on the game’s first turn. I think the competitive lists in the mix are going to be ones that rely either on dreadnoughts or bikes, as the improved stats on things like axes are more interesting than they are effective - 4 damage is really neat, but you’re paying a hundred points per model for a guy with 3 attacks. Ask any CSM player about Daemon Prince melee for a quick rundown of how disappointing that can be. 

Isaac: I have played one game so far into Custodes, I sent my army in, bounced, and then died. I think that will be indicative of all future games from here on out. That's fair, right? title: Lore Explainer: The Cosmology of The Lord of the Rings
content:
Tolkien’s universe has a relatively complicated internal cosmology that’s only really glimpsed from a distance in The Lord of the Rings, and doesn’t really feature at all in The Hobbit - although JRR Tolkien had been working on his “Legendarium” since World War I, it’s only really elaborated upon more fully in the Silmarillion, published in 1977, four years after his death, and expanded in the later anthologies Unfinished Tales (1980) and the History of Middle Earth (1983 - 1996), along with various unpublished material (Children of Hurin et al) compiled and edited by his son Christopher.

A lot of people don’t like The Silmarillion, calling it “impenetrable” and “impossibly dense”, but I believe that these people are wrong. In this article I’ll expand on the cosmology of Middle-Earth and answer questions like, “What is a Maiar?”, “Where do Dwarves come from?” and “What are Ents, anyway?”

Eru Iluvatar

Eru Iluvatar is, to all intents and purposes, the Tolkienised version of the Christian God - an eternal, omniscient, and omnipotent creator who existed before everything else and will continue to exist forever, regardless of what happens in the world, named Arda (of which Middle-Earth is a part). Illuvatar is the possessor of the Secret Fire, the flame that grants existence and life to everything else, and ultimately everything answers to him.

Illuvatar resides in the Timeless Halls, a place similar both to the primordial void and heaven, and from there he created the Ainur as his servants, formed from Illuvatar’s mind.

Ainulindale by Anna Kulisz Yoo

Ainur

The Ainur are immortal angelic beings, unsurprisingly similar to the Christian angels (this will be something of a running theme throughout this explainer), each born from a fragment of Ilúvatar’s mind - despite being ethereal beings born from the thoughts of the creator god, each of the Ainur nevertheless has a gender and familial relations, each determined by how Ilúvatar thought of them, brothers and sisters by dint of vibes, basically.

Once all the Ainur had been assembled in the Timeless Halls, Illuvatar began the most important aspect of the creation of a new species, teaching them how to make music. The newborn Ainur sang and sang their little hearts out, at first alone or in small groups, and later through larger ensembles. Through this singing and listening, each of the Ainur began to understand the minds of the other Ainur, and therefore formed a more complete picture of the mind of Ilúvatar. Not all the Ainur were happy campers, eager to please Illuvatar, though. An especially powerful Ainu named Melkor maliciously introduced discordant notes into the song (unmusical people discriminated against once again). When he was satisfied that the Ainur were decent enough singers, Iluvatar tasked them to collaborate with one another to create the Music of the Ainur, called the Ainulindalë in the later language of elves. The Ainulindalë was a complicated piece with three movements, and each of the Ainur were free to improvise around the themes set out by Iluvatar, weaving their own ideas into the great work. The music started out harmoniously enough, powerful and concordant, but the pride of Melkor caused him to add his own discord to the theme, causing conflict with the rest of the choir - some of the other Ainur took up Melkor’s discord and joined him in his rebellion against the perfect harmony of Ilúvatar’s vision, for Melkor desired possession of the Secret Fire and the power to create his own creatures to rival those of Ilúvatar.

The conflict between Illuvatar’s theme and Melkor’s discords built over the second movement, creating a turbulent sea of sound, crashing this way and that and causing dismay amongst the Ainur, many of whom stopped singing altogether in despair. One of the Ainur, Manwë, became a sort of principal proponent of Ilúvatar’s theme, taking the fight to his brother Melkor as they struggled for dominance over the music. Ilúvatar, acting as a sort of conductor, rose from his seat between each of the three themes to signal that it was time to change. The third theme was beautiful and sorrowful, and although Melkor rose up with a pompous, grandiose theme of his own in response, and although the discord between the themes shook the heavens, he was unable to overwhelm the beauty of Ilúvatar’s theme. Finally, Eru Illuvatar rose from his seat for a final time and ended the music with a deep and thunderous chord of his own.

As the Ainulindalë ceased, Eru Ilúvatar led the Ainur into the void and said to them, “Behold your music!” At once the Ainur were given a vision of the world and everything in it, including the Children of Ilúvatar, of whom they had no knowledge, and who had been added into the music with Ilúvatar’s voice alone. Following this vision, Ilúvatar said “Eä, let these things be!” and the material universe sprang into existence like the result of a colossal magic trick. Eä is the name given to the material universe, wherein sits Arda, the world of which Middle-Earth is a part.

Ilúvatar gave the Ainur permission to enter Eä to continue their work in shaping it; the mightiest who entered Arda are known as the Valar.

Valar

The Valar are essentially greater or arch-angels, powerful beings that are nevertheless subordinate to Ilúvatar himself. They are explicitly not gods or a pantheon in the polytheistic sense, although they may appear that way, and do have traits and characteristics similar to the pantheons of our own universe. Although they are spiritual beings and thus incorporeal, they can “wear” a physical form known as a Fana when they wish to appear to the children of Ilúvatar and other mortals in Arda.

They consist of six spousal pairs (yes, technically they’re all brothers and sisters of a kind, but they’re spiritual beings so it doesn’t count) and two unwed others:

  • Manwë and Varda
  • Aulë and Yavanna
  • Mandos and Vairë
  • Oromë and Vána
  • Lorien and Estë
  • Tulkas and Nessa
  • Nienna
  • Ulmo

As a subcategory, the most powerful of the Valar are known as the Arantar, or High Ones; these are Manwë, Ulmo, Aulë, Oromë, Mandos, Varda, Yavanna, and Nienna.

Let’s go through them one by one, shall we?

Manwe Sulimo, Lord of the Breath of Arda - Credit: Sepi Donne

Manwë

“Manwë is dearest to Ilúvatar and understands most clearly his purposes. He was appointed to be, in the fullness of time, the first of all Kings [...] his delight is in the winds and the clouds, and in all the regions of the air, from the heights to the depths, from the utmost borders of the Veil of Arda to the breezes that blow in the grass.“

Husband to Varda, Manwë is considered to be the king of the Valar, and is something of a Zeus character, although considerably less randy. His purview is the sky and the winds, and the birds are his servants. Some of the Maiar who came into his service took the form of mighty, sentient eagles that could speak and acted as messengers between Manwë and the people of Middle–Earth. His name in Sindarin is Aran Einior. When he appeared to mortals, his fana was that of a great king.

Varda Elentari, Credit: Sepi Donne

Varda

“With Manwë dwells Varda, Lady of the Stars, who knows all the regions of Eä. Too great is her beauty to be declared in the words of Men or of Elves; for the light of Ilúvatar lives still in her face. In light is her power and her joy.“

Manwë’s spouse and queen of the Valar. She’s the Valar referred to most often in the main Lord of the Rings books by her Sindarin name: Elbereth. Her beauty is beyond compare, her affiliation is with the stars and starlight, and the elves love her more than any other. Of all the Valar, Varda is the one that Melkor fears the most, as her gift of insight led her to be the first of the Valar to understand his nature and reject him. Manwë and Varda are a bit of a yin-yang power couple; through Varda’s light, Manwë is able to see through mist and darkness, and through Manwë, Varda is able to hear all the voices of creation. The phial with which Sam defeats the giant spider Shelob contains a tiny fragment of her light, which he activates by chanting a hymn to Varda known as A Elbereth Gilthoniel; Frodo also invokes this hymn at Weathertop as protection against the Witch-king of Angmar.

Aulë

“But the delight and pride of Aulë is in the deed of making, and in the thing made, and neither in possession nor in his own mastery, wherefore he gives and hoards not, and is free from care, passing ever on to some new work.”

The Silmarillion, "Ainulindalë"

Husband to Yavanna, Aulë is the Valar associated with materials, crafts, and invention. After the Ainulindalë, Aulë was responsible for the construction of Arda, which often brought him into conflict with Melkor, who envied Aulë’s creative ability and sought to deface his creations. In the time before the waking of the elves, Aulë created his own race of beings with attributes similar to his own, though as he did not possess the Secret Fire himself, Aulë was unable to give his creations true life independent of his own will. Illúvatar saw Aulë’s efforts and rebuked him, as the Ainulindalë was quite clear that the first to wake on Arda must be the first of Ilúvatar’s children, the Elves. Rather than show defiance like Melkor, Aulë submitted to the will of Ilúvatar and sadly raised his hammer to destroy his creations. As he did so, they cried out and cowered in fear as Ilúvatar, taking pity on them, imbued the Children of Aulë with true life, essentially adopting them as his own. This new race, known as the Dwarves, was thus put into a deep sleep, only to awaken after the emergence of the elves.

Yavanna - Credit: Mathias Moor

Yavanna

“She is the lover of all things that grow in the earth, and all their countless forms she holds in her mind, from the trees like towers in forests long ago to the moss upon stones or the small and secret things in the mould.”

Wife of Aulë, Yavanna is known to the elves as the Giver of Fruits, for her responsibility is to everything that grows from the ground (seems like a pretty massive responsibility; she must be very busy). Her domain and demeanour are similar to that of Demeter. Only slightly lesser in power and reverence than Varda, Yavanna is said to be the planter of the first seeds in Arda, and the plants her conceptions and creations. When she wears a fana, she often appears in the form of a tall woman in green crowned with the sun, or as a tree. When her husband Aulë created the dwarves, she feared that they would cut down all the trees in Arda, becoming even more alarmed when her husband informed her that Ilúvatar’s children (Elves and Men) would also need to cut down trees. She took her concerns to Manwë, asking in despair whether any of her creations would ever be free of the dominion of others, exclaiming: “Would that the trees might speak on behalf of all things that have roots, and punish those that wrong them!” This utterance of Yavanna took root in Manwë’s mind, and as it unfolded, Ilúvatar responded to her plea by promising that he would create beings to defend the forests and shepherd the trees, the Ents.

Yavanna and Aule had an odd relationship. After receiving Illuvatar’s promise that the trees would have their guardians, she went to him at work in his smithy and said, “Now let thy children beware! For there shall walk a power in the forests whose wrath they will arouse at their peril,” to which he replied, “Nonetheless, they will have need of wood,” and kept on smithing, an odd pair indeed.

Ulmo - credit: Nahar Doa

Ulmo

“Ulmo is the Lord of Waters. He is alone. He dwells nowhere long, but moves as he will in all the deep waters about the Earth or under the Earth.”

Ulmo is essentially a kind of Poseidon/Oceanus analogue, responsible for the seas, bays, rivers, and waters of Arda. Along with Manwë, Aulë, and Yavanna, Ulmo took part in the physical creation of the world, fabricating the oceans and the rains that water the land. He’s an unusual Valar in that he has no spouse and doesn’t live with the others on solid ground, preferring to spend his time in the deep oceans of his creation. Ulmo rarely wears a fana, but when he does, he appears as a terrible oceanic apparition “like a mounting wave”, wearing a dark foam-crested helmet and mail that shimmers between silver and green. When he speaks, his voice is as deep as the ocean. Although Ulmo might seem like a bit of a misanthropic loner, he has a deep love for the Children of Ilúvatar and has never forsaken them, acting as a protector even when the other Valar seemed to have abandoned them. The elves say that Ulmo’s waters are the veins of the earth, and therefore news comes to him of the needs and grief of the children that even Manwë cannot hear. He’s also the best musician among them, and elves believe they can hear the distant echo of the Ainulindalë in the waters.

Mandos - Credit: Eduardo Dekamaster

Namo and Vaire

Namo, also known as Mandos, is the creepiest of the Valar. He and his brother Irmo form a duet known as the Fëanturi, whose domains are the mastery of spirits. As a quasi-Hades analogue, he is the keeper of the House of the Dead and the Valar who knows everything that has happened and almost everything that is going to happen, except that which Iluvatar has yet to decide. Although Namo’s duty is a grim one, he is neither malicious nor evil. The domain of Mandos functions as a kind of cosmic waiting room, where the souls of slain elves are gathered to await their eventual reincarnation. Not much is written about his wife, Vaire, the Weaver, but the halls of Mandos are decorated with tapestries woven by Vaire that depict everything that has ever happened, although presumably she leaves out the parts where the characters go to the toilet.

Nienna, by Antonio Vinci

Nienna

Nienna, the Lady of Pity, is the sister of Namo and Irmo, and is the Valar concerned with grief, sorrow, and the endurance thereof. She’s a maudlin sort, although she does not weep for herself, she mourns rather the tragedies and sorrows of others, and the hurts of the world. From the beginning, Nienna was sorrowful, mixing a thread of lamentation into the Ainulindale, preemptively mourning the sorrows yet to come. She seldom visits other Valar, save for her brother Mandos - when she visits his halls, she cries with the spirits of the dead and provides comfort and strength as they wait for their turn at reincarnation.

Oromë the Hunter - Credit: Daniel Govar

Oromë and Vana

Oromë, also known in Sindarin as Tauron, is the huntsman of the Valar and is tasked with hunting and killing of monsters and fell beasts that plague the Children of Ilúvatar in Middle-earth. He was the first of the Valar to discover the elves after they awoke, and gave them the name Eldar. His wife is Vana, Ever-Young, the younger sister of Yavanna, who is most closely associated with flowers and youthfulness. She’s a bit of a Disney princess character; it is said that all flowers open and bloom at her coming, and all the birds sing.

Irmo and Este

The brother of Namo, Irmo, also known as Lorien, is given the title Master of Dreams, and as you might expect, his halls are a pretty trippy but relaxing place. He imparts visions upon the elves to guide them. Este, given the epithet “the gentle”, is the wife of Irmo and the Valar concerned with the healing of hurts and rest. So great are her powers that the other Valar visit the halls of Irmo seeking relaxation and refreshment.

Tulkas by Nahar Doa

Tulkas and Nessa

Tulkas, the Valiant, is a sort of Hercules-like figure. Of all the Valar, he’s physically the strongest and loves to engage in feats of strength and prowess, fighting with no weapons other than his hands. He doesn’t ride any kind of steed, since he can run faster than anything and apparently has infinite stamina. Although he is extremely strong and violent, Tulkas is not “dreadful”. Instead, he is a merry and boisterous character, laughing loudly while fighting. He embodies the purest Himbo qualities: he is a stout friend and not easily roused to anger, but neither learns from the past nor thinks of the future and is described as “of no avail as a councillor”, yeowch. During one of the wars against evil, Tulkas wrestled Melkor and threw him down on his face. Badass.

Nessa is the wife of Tulkas and sister of Orome. Not much is written about her, except that she’s a very fast runner, deer follow her about, and she’s great at dancing.

Maiar

The Maiar are a lesser kind of Ainur compared to the Valar, angels to their archangels, and as such are the servants and helpers of the Valar. Unlike the Valar, the number of Maiar is unknown, but safe to say there are quite a lot of them, often occupying niches subordinate to the major Valar they serve - for example: Ossë is a Maiar known as the Master of the Coasts, who delights in storms and the roaring of waves, and as such is the vassal of Ulmo, along with his wife Uinen, who is beloved by mariners for her ability to calm the waters stirred into rage by Ossë. Other notable Maiar include Balrogs and the Istari (known by men as Wizards).

Credit: Sepi Donne

Istari

The Istari is the name given to five Maiar dispatched by the Valar, with Eru’s consent, to assist the peoples of Middle-Earth in resisting Sauron. The last time the Valar themselves went to war against Melkor’s forces, they smashed the place up like a rough pub on a Saturday night, so sending some subordinates was probably a smart move. The Istari were clad in the physical forms of elderly men, not just fana, so they were able to feel pain, greed, joy, hunger, and everything else that makes a human. In addition to this kind of forced empathising with men and elves, their physical bodies could be killed. In case you were thinking that the Valar placed too many restrictions on the Istari, they were also forbidden from attempting to force men to do their bidding, instead relying on their abilities to persuade and advise. Honestly, we could write a whole article about the Istari by themselves, so I’ll just give a short précis for each here.

Saruman

The White, originally known as Curumo, was a Maiar pupil of Aulë (just like Sauron; Aulë really had rotten luck with his choice of disciples). Saruman was described as the wisest of the Istari and their chief. Saruman was proud and resentful of the apparent favour bestowed upon his subordinate Gandalf, first by Varda and then by the elf Cirdan, who entrusted to him the ring of power Narya. Fails in his mission to defeat Sauron after becoming corrupted by a desire for power.

Gandalf

The Grey, then the White, originally known as Olórin, was a Maiar pupil of Irmo who became associated with Varda, Nienna, and Manwë at various points. Olórin was chosen to journey to Middle-earth as one of the Istari but was reluctant, as he was scared of Sauron (with good reason), but Manwë ordered him to go anyway, saying that his fear made him an ideal candidate to assist the Elves and Men. Travelled far among men and learned much from the people of Middle-earth, ultimately using both his wisdom and empathy to assist in the destruction of Sauron and the salvation of men.

Radagast

The Brown, originally known as Aiwendil, was a Maiar pupil of Yavanna and was included in the Istari’s mission at her insistence, which was probably a bit embarrassing for him, like your mum insisting that the other kids let you play with them. As you might expect from a disciple of Yavanna, he’s very, very interested in plants and animals, less so in elves and men. Although he assists Gandalf in a few ways, ultimately he fails in his mission after becoming too distracted by his special interest.

The Blue Wizards

A weird bit of ephemera, the only indication that the remaining two wizards exist in the text of The Lord of the Rings comes when Saruman makes mention of “the rods of the five wizards”, suggesting that there must be two more wizards than the three previously mentioned. That’s it! That’s the only mention at all in the main body of the story, outside of paratext. In the paratextual “Essay on the Istari”, Tolkien mentions the two “Blue Wizards” travelled much farther east and perhaps south than the other wizards; however:

“What success they had I do not know; but I fear that they failed, as Saruman did, though doubtless in different ways; and I suspect they were founders or beginners of secret cults and “magic” traditions that outlasted the fall of Sauron.”

Their names and associations are a bit murky; in some writings Tolkien refers to them as Alatar and Pallando, and suggests they are Maiar of Orome (which perhaps makes them suited to range farther than the other wizards, since Orome was also very widely travelled in Middle-earth), while another connects Pallando to Mandos and Nienna. Further writing in Unfinished Tales suggests that Alatar was selected by Orome, and took Pallando along as a friend, which I think is quite nice.

Even then, Tolkien changed his mind often on who and what the Blue Wizards were and their particular deeds. In later writings, he calls them Morinehtar and Rómestámo, Darkness-Slayer and East-Helper and changes his mind as to whether they “failed”; in one of the last things he wrote, Tolkien states:

“Their task was to circumvent Sauron: to bring help to the few tribes of Men that had rebelled from Melkor-worship, to stir up rebellion ... and after his first fall to search out his hiding (in which they failed) and to cause [?dissension and disarray] among the dark East ... They must have had very great influence on the history of the Second Age and Third Age in weakening and disarraying the forces of East ... who would both in the Second Age and Third Age otherwise have ... outnumbered the West.“

So it seems that rather than being abject failures, Tolkien decided that the two Blue Wizards played a great role in keeping a great chunk of Easterlings out of the wars altogether as provocateurs, diplomats, and destabilisers. In doing so, he massively adjusts the chronology as well; in this later telling, the Blue Wizards didn’t arrive with the other Istari at the start of the Third Age, but had been active in Middle-earth since the middle of the Second Age. In short: who knows? Even Tolkien didn’t seem to know.

Luthien Singing Before Morgoth - Credit: Sepi Donne

Melkor

Melkor is the most powerful of Ilúvatar’s Ainur, and yet he rebelled against the creator and was booted out of “heaven”. Sound familiar? That’s right: in so far as Ilúvatar is the Christian God, Melkor is essentially Middle-Earth’s version of John Milton’s Satan, the fallen angel.

After Ilúvatar and the rest of the Valar gave him a dressing-down for introducing discord into the Ainulindalë, Melkor corrupted a bunch of the lesser Ainur (Maiar) into following him in his rebellion. Once Ea had been created, Melkor was one of the Ainur who begged permission to enter the physical world and shape it - though in secret, Melkor desired power and to dominate the children of Iluvatar when they awoke. In retrospect, the alarm bells should have started to ring when the Valar arrived on the earth (Arda) and Melkor declared himself to be the ruler of the world (uh oh, never a good sign). Manwë, his brother, was a little perturbed by this declaration and summoned a bunch more Ainur to shore up their defences, including his wife Varda.

Melkor was (understandably) afraid of his Sister-in-Law and bounced off to the fringes of the world and spent a while in the distant, remote parts of the world, brooding and scheming. As the Valar began to shape the world and make it beautiful, Melkor spent his precious time trying to sabotage their works in whatever way he could, much to their chagrin. 

Since the sun and moon wouldn’t exist for a long while, Aulë built two very large lamps to light the dwelling-place of the Valar, an island called Almaren. These ginormous lamps on ginormous poles lit up the world with a perfect, even light, and the Valar lived happily on their island. Meanwhile, Melkor, together with his Maiar and monstrous creations, dug out a huge fortress called Utumno, from where his aura of corruption seeped out into the world like a bad smell from a rotten carcass.

Being a dickhead, Melkor took it upon himself to destroy the lamps. Waiting until Tulkas was asleep and the Valar were having a party, Melkor and company attacked both lamps at once, knocking them down and extinguishing the lights. The falling lamps made such a mess of the world that it was shattered, leaving behind big craters that eventually became inland seas. The Valar were, understandably, cheesed off by the destruction of their lamps and their houses, so they upped sticks and moved to the western continent, leaving Middle-earth to Melkor for the time being. With his dominance over Middle-earth secured for the time being, Melkor started pumping out his corruption, along with monstrous, perverse mockeries of natural creatures; presumably, he was laughing and twirling his moustache the whole time.

When the elves awoke beneath the stars, some of them ran away from Oromë; Melkor snatched a few of them and dragged them back to Utumno. It’s a big debate, and Tolkien never really settled on an answer in his lifetime, but plenty of readers believe that these captive elves were subject to immense cruelty at the hands of Melkor, who used a combination of torture and forced breeding to turn them into Orcs, as a mockery of the Children of Iluvatar and in mockery of Iluvatar himself.

Eventually, skipping over a lot of intervening drama, the Valar, fighting alongside the elves and men, managed to capture Melkor (or Morgoth, as he became known), chain him up, and throw him through the Doors of Night, casting him into the eternal void, there to do no more harm to the Children of Iluvatar. Even so, prophecy says he’ll come back at the end of days to cause trouble once again.
