title: Futuristic Rare Mew and Mewtwo Pokémon cards are now worth less than their full art counterparts
content:
Futuristic Rares are the headline new art treatment introduced in the Pokémon TCG's 30th Celebration set. Cards in this art style are depicted as though they're made of chrome, with the energy card symbols displayed in the background behind them. Only four Futuristic Rare Pokémon cards currently exist, and only two of them have been released: Mew and Mewtwo ex (the two Futuristic Rare Pikachus are debuting in the 30th Celebration Ultra-Premium Collection, which releases in November). Yet, for all of the hype behind this new card type, both Mew and Mewtwo are now available for cheaper prices than their full art counterparts.

It's hard to overstate how incredibly hyped members of the Pokémon TCG community were for Futuristic Rares. Data from TCGplayer demonstrates that when price tracking for these cards first began on August 10th, Mewtwo ex had an expected value of $1000 (£755), while Mew ex was valued at $3.2 thousand dollars (£2.4 thousand pounds).

More than a month separated these cards getting listed, and their release, as 30th Celebration came out on September 16th. Because of this, the values assigned to these cards were highly speculative. It's natural that the prices of cards dip once the set they are included in comes out, and more copies make their way into the hands of players, but in this instance the values of Futuristic Rare Mew and Mewtwo ex took a dramatic tumble.

At the time of writing, Futuristic Rare Mew has a market price of $62 (£46), while Futuristic Rare Mewtwo has a market price of $50 (£37). In both instances, this represents a drop of more than 95% compared to their anticipated value prior to release. Not only that, but it also gives them a price lower than their Special Illustration Rare (SIR) counterparts. SIR Mew ex is currently valued at $88 (£66), while SIR Mewtwo ex has a market price of $57 (£43).

This isn't the first time that a fancy new art treatment has been upstaged by the reliable charm of full art cards. The shining Gold Mega Hyper Rares, introduced at the start of the Mega Evolution series in September of 2025 famously did not retain their position of monetary pre-eminence for long, and are now routinely less valuable than their SIR counterparts.

What kind of extravagant art treatments would you like to see in the future? And do you think that Special Illustration Rares will ever be upstaged as the premier option? Tell us your views in the Wargamer Discord.

title: Black Library Readers’ Hall of Fame: The Winners of 2018, and Class of 2019
content:
The Black Library Readers’ Hall of Fame is Tabletop Battles’s long-term, reader-participation initiative to recognize those novels that have “cultural, historical, or aesthetic significance” to the Black Library. Through the votes of readers as well as our community panel of community voices, we’ll examine the entire history of the Black Library, induct the latest winners, and vote for the next round’s candidates every other week.

Welcome back to the Class of 2018 Edition of the Black Library Readers’ Hall of Fame! At this point in Black Library history, the original Horus Heresy is winding down, the Age of Sigmar is heating up, and 40K is firing on all cylinders. An impressive seven books from that year have been selected by the community for induction to the Hall, as well as one author getting in for the first time!

As a reminder, if you're really enjoying this project and want to see it from a different angle, the companion piece, The Hall Monitor, runs over at my Substack, The Warhammer Wordforge. A cross between a director's commentary and behind-the-scenes look, each installment we dive a little deeper into a particular element of the Readers' Hall of Fame project. Hope to see you there!

The Envelope Please

Now, let's get to the stars of the show, the books inducted for 2018!

Keri, The WH40K Book Club: "I really don't like the Death Guard. A lot about them creeps me out and, quite frankly, grosses me out. The Lords of Silence did nothing to change my perspective, and yet, Chris Wraight captivated me with his Lords of Silence. It was gross, it was funny, it was intriguing, and it brought me a whole new view on the Traitor Marines in general. I'm eagerly awaiting a sequel, because there's no way we're done with Vorx's story. I'm not done with Vorx's story."

Jay, Tabletop Battles and the Warhammer Wordforge: "With The Lords of Silence, Wraight helped rewrite the book on the Death Guard similar to how Aaron Dembski-Bowden with the Night Lords. These were hardly one-note rot fiends, but rather deeply developed characters that balanced their physical horror with a pious and philosophical perspective. Beyond being a rightly-deserved fan favorite, the book helped expand the way the Traitor Legions are understood and portrayed."

Jay, Tabletop Battles and the Warhammer Wordforge: "The Magos not only served as a sort of connective bridge between his trio of Inquisition trilogies, but it stood as a terrific story in its own right. A detective tale with those elements of cosmic horror and Imperial intrigue that Abnett has mastered over the course of his career, it showcased one of the canon's legends at the top of his game. The original Eisenhorn trilogy was told in the first person, and by switching to the third-person here Abnett forced readers to reckon with Gregor Eisenhorn not as how he saw himself, but how the rest of the universe did."

Jay, Tabletop Battles and the Warhammer Wordforge: "Throughout the Readers' Hall of Fame project, we've typically seen the first book of a trilogy stand in for the entire series when being assessed for Hall inclusion. Because the middle book is built off the first one, the bar is higher. But sometimes that middle book manages to stand on its own feet too, as is the case with Guy Haley's Plague War. There weren't a lot of books that brought the lore "forward" like this, but Haley rose to the challenge with some of the most memorable Primarch confrontation writing we've seen to date. And given that we're at the tail end of the Horus Heresy, that's saying something!"

Jay, Tabletop Battles and the Warhammer Wordforge: "Though their adventures began in the novella City of Secrets, this was the first novel appearance of gritty duo Armand Callis and Hanniver Toll. While they'd go on to return in 2024's Callis & Toll by David Annandale, Horth's swashbuckling, pulpy adventure through the jungles of Ghur was filled with terrific action and characterization. A story on an "ordinary" human scale (much as Imperial Guard stories tend to be in the 40K setting), this one was a standout success for early Age of Sigmar fiction."

Gus, Black Library Subreddit: "Well deserved. This is Callis and Toll’s first full length adventure after meeting in City of Secrets. What’s cool about this one is we get to travel the Realm of Beasts, rather than being stuck in and around Excelsis. Nick North understands the setting of Age of Sigmar well and writes a great catch me if you can/treasure hunting adventure where we get to see a growing friendship between the titular characters that personally endeared me to them and made me a lifelong fan. Add an elf tomb raider and you get one of the best adventure novels in the Black Library.

There’s pirates- Khorn Pirates!!! And Seraphon!!! And Kharadron!!! Some of the character interactions are hilarious. Truly a deserving hall of famer."

Jay, Tabletop Battles and the Warhammer Wordforge: "As the end of the Heresy approaches the era of the Siege of Terra, John French delivered a masterpiece ensemble work that pulled together a number of different narrative threads. A story with tremendous narrative weight as well as French's attention to psychological detail, there's a reason it's the final book in the ongoing Horus Heresy Saga reprint series."

Aasa Timonen, The Warhammer Scholar: "Soul Wars is one of those Black Library books that were published as tie-in for the then current new edition of the game, sharing name with the 2nd Edition starter set for Age of Sigmar. This does not diminish the book in slightest - in fact, it is one of the best introduction books into the Mortal Realms. Josh Reynolds makes the immortal Stormcast Eternals feel achingly human with their doubts, fears, and lingering memories of what they used to be. He does that while also writing a thrilling siege story which starts as massive clash of armies, and ends as almost private and personal fight over the soul of a one person."

JordanSorcery: "The early years of the Age of Sigmar featured plenty of controversial moments, especially with regards to the lore of the Mortal Realms. It’s only mildly contentious to suggest that it was not until Black Library’s fiction writers had been given room to explore that the shape of this new universe, and a strong narrative thread, really began to emerge.

"Published in 2018 Josh Reynolds’ Soul Wars might be amongst the first almost universally agreed upon successes in the setting. A story centred on the machinations of everyone’s favourite mean-spirited former silent movie star ready for his close-up, Nagash, and his long brewing war against chopped unc Sigmar, Soul Wars would introduce a completely new cast of characters and put them through their paces in dynamic fashion. Fortunately though it wasn’t just mindless action, instead offering insights into the rival powers at play in this war of gods and monsters.

"For many this was the strongest outing in the setting since Reynolds’ own early work in the Realm Gate Wars. It put a deeper, darker spin on the battles that would follow in the game itself, and set the stage for what is still one of the most memorable conflicts in Age of Sigmar’s real-time history."

Gus, Black Library Subreddit: "Probably one of the best Black Library novels. ADB gave us a different kind of Space Marine tale, one told from a human perspective that really drives down how far from base line humanity the emperor’s angels are, and at the same time, how much humanity they have in them. I know, sounds confusing, but believe me when I say, it’s what makes this book so brilliant. It is a very intense, very graphic, very emotional novel. For me it was one of those that have you staring at the wall in silence after putting the book down.

"Dembski-Bowden always does a great job of writing interactions between humans and Astartes, and showing the emotional and psychological toll of the scenarios where these two groups must bands together to avoid annihilation. The book also continues the story of the Celestial Lions from ADB’s novella Blood and Fire, itself a follow up to Grimaldus’s story from Helsreach."

Jay, Tabletop Battles and the Warhammer Wordforge: "While Dembski-Bowden has a strong reputation for writing sympathetically deep portrayals of the Traitor Legions, here he gives us his take on a Loyalist one- with a twist. With the Cicatrix Maledictum rending the universe in twain, the Emperor's Spears must discover what it means to be a light in the darkness, when you don't know how much light is even left. Dembski-Bowden's emotional resonance and masterful worldbuilding are on full display here, with one of the era's truly outstanding offerings."

Congratulations to all the worthy winners, and especially first-time winner Nick Horth!

title: The DnD versions of WoW classes just got revealed, and it's underwhelming
content:
The crossover between Dungeons and Dragons and World of Warcraft is a milestone moment in the fantasy gaming fandom. After all, it's a full circle moment for WoW, itself inspired by the DnD of old in both lore and game design.  Eyes were particularly drawn towards how Wizards of the Coast will approach WoW's interpretation of RPG classes, especially direct comparisons such as Rogue and Druid. The latest showcase for the crossover enlightens players on those details.

All 13 of World of Warcraft's classes have been converted into  DnD classes for the crossover. As in WoW, specializations are available, granting unique spell loadouts on top of new spells inspired by WoW.  Rather than each class being built from the ground up, however, WotC opted to change up existing DnD classes and used them as the foundation for WoW classes.

Here's a quick list of every WoW class, alongside significant changes made to their DnD counterparts.

  • Death Knight (Hero Class) - Paladin, new Oath of the Ebon Blade subclass, new runeforging mechanics
  • Demon Hunter (Hero Class) - Ranger, new Demon Hunter subclass , new spells
  • Evoker (Hero Class) - Sorcerer, modified version of Draconic Sorcery subclass, new spells from specializations
  • Druid - Druid with unique statblocks for the Beast Forms, certain subclasses flavored as specializations
  • Hunter - Ranger, new Pet Specialization feature for Beast Mastery, new trap spells, certain subclasses flavored as specializations
  • Mage - Wizard, new feats &  elemental spells, certain subclasses flavored as specializations
  • Monk - Monk, new feats unique to Brewmaster specialization, certain subclasses flavored as specializations
  • Paladin - Paladin, new Oath of the Holy subclass, certain subclasses flavored as specializations
  • Priest - Cleric, new Discipline Domain and Shadow Domain subclasses, certain subclasses flavored as specializations
  • Rogue - Rogue, certain subclasses flavored as specializations
  • Shaman - Barbarian, new Totem mechanic, new Path of the Elements subclass, certain subclasses flavored as specializations
  • Warlock - Warlock, certain subclasses flavored as specializations
  • Warrior - New maneuvers for Battle Master,  certain subclasses flavored as specializations

On a personal note as a fan of DnD and WoW, this approach to the classes is mildly disappointing. While I'm a huge fan of big swings such as Death Knight and Demon Hunter, others feel phoned in. Rogue is particularly egregious. I simply do not agree that Swashbuckler is a valid representation of WoW's Outlaw Rogue. The former is an artful dodger, striking with wit and sword precisely, whilst the latter is a literal flurry of violent blades in combat.

I'd expect, at the very least, a new subclass focused on the fast-paced and complex DPS playstyle of Outlaw. Roll the Bones would have been a hilarious way to incorporate a Wild Magic-esque twist to the Rogue play style, offering random buffs in combat. Hopefully, once the full sourcebook makes its way out of the DnD release schedule, there are more surprises in store for fans of the fantasy franchises.

You can read more details on the WoW x DnD classes over at  DnDBeyond.

Have some thoughts about the crossover? The Wargamer Discord is open for your take on Azeroth's incursion into the Forgotten Realms.

Old Dark Angels close off their incredible early 11th run with one final showdown, facing off against a very hard-hitting Genestealer build in a Recon mirror. Gather Intel has some fairly unusual scoring dynamics, and both sides have some angles on exploiting that. The good news for Cults is that you can score very flexibly here - front-loading points onto turns two and three is very doable, and if the Dark Angels ever let them sneak onto their home and Action, that locks in a bunch of points. The bad news is that the reverse is also true - if the Dark Angels play a cautious, grindy game, they can rack up points later once most of the Cults are dead. That is a bit riskier into Cults than almost anyone else, because it's quite unlikely you'll manage to fully eliminate them, and this is a mission where the right unit in the wrong place can create a massive point swing.

I think what ultimately pushes this one towards the Dark Angels (apart from the sheer brutality of the army) is how difficult it is for the Cults to deny them access to central objectives with split centres. As long as the Dark Angels get their 6VP turn one, they have so many routes to 100 and such a killing advantage that it's hard to see the Cults managing to make sufficient headway. The Angels have to somewhat overcommit to protecting their home to avoid a slip up, but otherwise focusing on carving up the Genestealers while the Lion and Samael's units sweep key pieces off the table should be more than enough for the win, which does seem to be how this played out. Interesting one to analyse - this shows how big a difference the change to split the centres on this mission made, helping grindier Recon armies win the mirror.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Wyldwood Box and Miniatures
content:
Wyldwood is the newest board game from Tabletop Titans; a Stone Age era game with a unique style played on a hex-based board. One of the things that distinguishes this game from the field is its scale: Wyldwood uses 60mm display miniatures for the models. Additionally, the game eschews dice in favor of a mix of cards from a deck and individualized abilities on your character boards. If you've been looking for a hex-based game with the kinds of miniatures you'd expect to enter a painting competition with, this game might be a good fit for you.

We'd like to thank Tabletop Titans for providing us with a preview copy of the upcoming Kickstarter boxes for review.

So far, we've had the chance to see two of the factions from Wyldwood's Kickstarter campaign. In this article, we're going to explore painting the Leafsong Nomads, unpack some of the contents of the Kickstarter boxes, and look at how the game plays.

There's a lot of hype around Wyldwood, and a lot of that can be traced back to the game's Adepticon debut. Tabletop Titans are currently running a Kickstarter campaign, which is live now so make sure to check it out.

Wyldwood- Blake Law

Wyldwood- Blake Law

Wyldwood- Blake Law

Wyldwood- Blake Law

Models

Blake Law: These models are as good as it gets. Consider Wyldwood to be the new top tier standard for sculpts and casting. The sculpts are done by Creature Caster, which is widely known for their insane detail on resin models. It carries a lot of name recognition, and with good reason. These miniatures have been cast in Unicool, which is a resin/plastic hybrid. There is plenty of Unicool reviews on this site, so make sure to look them up!  In the end, you have a product that is sculpted by one of the best in the industry and cast with one of the best materials on the market. It assembles seamlessly. I did no additional work on any of these miniatures. Each piece typically has one gate to cut off. There are no mold lines on any of these models. I had no issues with any of the pieces fitting together. You have no instruction manual on how to build these, and that is because they are so intuitive and easy; you cannot get better than this in terms of assembly and ease. Unicool sometimes has an issue with bending of parts that require reheating. I had no issues at all in that regard with Wyldwood models. The larger models in the line (typically the leaders) are massive. This can be somewhat of an issue if your work space is small. I had to upgrade my lightbox space to be able to capture them in photo!

The Box Contents

Blake Law: I got access to two of the single faction starter boxes.  I will be discussing them in general terms. If you're looking for more specific details on specific cards, stay tuned: We'll be reviewing those in a separate article, soon.

I want to discuss the box that they come in first.  The art is actually spectacular.  There is even quality art lining the inside of the box.  It is a nice  touch that gives the game a high end feel.  I was scared to haul my models inside the lid (as I typically do) because I did not want to damage it.  You get three cardboard punch outs that contain several key components of the game.  The first two are terrain feature punch outs.  These make four trees and two bushes.  They match the art style of the game perfectly and are quite vibrant  (see photo).  I did not notice any issues with these punching out.  The next punch out contains the tokens for status effects.  The art is again very on par with the rest of the game.  I did notice some issues with the edges of tokens not punching quite perfect.  When I go back and finish my Leafsong Nomads, I will be using an exacto blade to clean the edges.  I also like to line the edges of cardboard with black sharpie.  It always gives these kind of games a nicer feel on tabletop.  You get a cardboard dial for each character in your faction.  They include the rivets to complete each of these dials.  As you complete parts of the character dials, you get to use the cute little spirit creatures to fill the empty spots on dials.

The Kickstarter campaign has the option to get the printed versions (versus the standard cardboard tokens).  I highly recommend this, as it adds a value of visual aesthetic to the game.  You get two decks per faction.  The print quality is very nice, and you will probably want to get these in sleeves to protect the art.  The last component is the game board itself.  It comes folded, and has a back side which is a map of the world.  It is a very nice touch.  There is a neoprene mat that you can get on the Kickstarter, and I would again go for this if you plan to play a lot of games.  While the mat is a durable paper material, it will very likely fail over time.  Also, I intended to frame the backside map over my game table!

The two starter boxes that I reviewed came with five and seven models.  I believe five is around the standard for most of the factions.  Leafsong Nomads have five base characters, and two creatures which operate off of the Wyldspeaker's abilities.  Leafsong Nomads come with Enduanna, The Wispwarden (leader), Wyldspeaker, Boneblade Alpha, Loresinger, and Wyrdbow Sentinel.  You get two creatures in addition (Sabrecat and Thistlehare), which play off the Wyldspeaker.  The Emberhold Ascended box comes with Alulim, The First King (leader), Fellbrand Woodsman, Ashbolt Marksman, Fuelwright Master, and Boughrunner.  I want to reiterate how massive these models are.  They could be easily used by someone looking to paint a competition caliber piece.  If you have not dealt with 60mm before, it is a ton of fun.  See the pictures below of all the amazing models!

Emma: So Blake's given the detailed specs here, and I'm only going to chip in to back up his comments on the aesthetics. The models absolutely rip. The Stone Age theming is subtle outside of the dwarf faction, Urscar Kindred, as the other factions either have heavy fantasy elements or are deliberately up-teched (the human Emberhold Ascended), but definitely present. If you're not a fan of painting metal, this is the game for you. 

The large scale allows for oodles of detail and character, as do the sculpted bases. As a Nightwood Covenant (orcs) player, I'm naturally biased towards their stuff, with their gorgeous nature theming and dynamic effects (the Stormwarden's lightning springs to mind), but every range has something to love. The visual identity of each faction and model is distinct, and I echo Blake's comments that this game is a painter's dream. Equally, for the non-painters among us, I reckon you could easily achieve a serviceable job with way less time than it would take you to finish a couple squads in a smaller scale game. It has a nice balance for accessibility of a low floor for entry and a high ceiling for improvement.

Paint

Blake Law: I started off by priming the models with Color Forge Spray Matt Black.  I then use my airbrush to apply the green over the models.  This was a progression of Pro Acryl Black Green, Pro Acryl Green, then Pro Acryl Bright Yellow Green.  Then, I applied skin tones with an airbrush on every model except the Sabrecat.  This was a progression of Pro Acryl Tan Flesh, Pro Acryl Bright Dark Warm Flesh, and then Pro Acryl Bright Shadow Flesh.   At this point, I went back in with a dry brush and lightly reinforced the brightest points of the green and the flesh tones.  The next step was applying the bone tone on the antlers and other antler-like parts.  This was done with Pro Acryl Green Brown, blended into Pro Acryl Bone, blended with Pro Acryl Bright Ivory.  The key is to blend the edges of the colors, but not so much that it's a true wet blend.  You want it to be a distinct color on each part, tapering to the edge.  I use Citadel Colour Contrast Skeleton Horde over that final blend.  You want to make sure you take some off the brightest points, as it will wash out the blend otherwise.

For the wooden components, I start with Pro Acryl Mahogany.  I blend that into a 50/50 mix of Mahogany and Pro Acryl Bright Pale Yellow.   I finish it off by fine lining Bright Pale Yellow over the blend.  The final step is applying Scalecolor Inktense Wood.  This gives it a blended look and brings the yellow back to a brown tone.  For my orange hair, I use a progression of Army Painter Fanatic Molten Lava, Army Painter Fanatic Lava Orange, and Army Painter Fanatic Glowing Inferno.

For my feathers, I use a stippling technique with my brush.  This is done with the colors Pro Acryl Light Umber, Pro Acryl Dark Ivory, to AK Interactive White I went back in and did some edge highlighting with the Bright Yellow Green over all the green plant parts of the models.  I applied an OSL with Reaper Master Series Clear Magenta.  This was done mostly with airbrush, but I go back in and clean up parts I want more glow on with a brush.

The final touch is the rocks on the bases.  I start with AK Interactive Black on all my bases.  I work this up with Pro Acryl Dark Neutral Grey,  Pro Acryl Neutral Grey, to Pro Acryl Bone.

Gameplay

Emma: My time to shine. 

I've been jamming game after game of this since I became aware of the Kickstarter, and would encourage anyone who wishes to give it a go to grab TTS and play around a bit. This isn't a review of the TTS mod, though, but of the game itself, and I am extremely happy with it. Rather than going into a deep dive on how the game works, which you can find on the Kickstarter itself in various forms, I'm instead going to give an overview of the mechanics, and then get into my opinions thereupon.

First things first; this is a diceless game. Variance is decided with three decks.

The first is the Location deck, a neutral fixed deck that determines terrain placement. This strikes a good middle ground between changing up the game-to-game experience, with different deployment zones and terrain locations. It's always four trees and two rocks at the time of writing, so it's not War and Peace to set up, but it does make a surprising amount of difference where things are. I like the balance struck here.

The second is the Omens deck, another neutral fixed deck that sets out where Wisps spawn (forest friends you collect to score points), and any environmental effects (such as a monster attack, flash flood, or portents of bloodshed). These have varying levels of impact, but are always relevant because of how much Wisps matter. At the time of writing, the exact rules are being tweaked, but are close to their final form.

The third is your own deck, which you construct from a faction card pool. Deck size is 30, so outcomes are reasonably consistent, but not so consistent that you can expect to do the same things every game. You pick an always-on ability for your faction from three options, like a detachment rule or formation from 40k/AoS, and then 30+ cards to form the deck itself. If you have passing familiarity with card games, the deckbuilding will make intuitive sense to you, but equally any wargamer can jump right in and know what things are doing. There's a whole bunch of depth and variation to it, and you could easily get completely different experiences each game even with the same deck, never mind if you mix it up a bit every so often.

Cards are balanced by their Fate cost, copy limit, and which models can use them. All have access to some generic faction options, while each model also has its own specific picks. For example, there's an any-model card in the Urscar Kindred dwarfs that lets a model make an extra move, while their leader model, Rurik, has access to a card that lets him move and then also maul someone with his giant bear.

The game has an online deckbuilder [link] with all the rules freely available, and I've spent a lot of time just jamming decks together. It only takes a few minutes per deck, and the cards themselves are very short - no more than 20 words per card, and most have fewer than that - so the skill expression isn't in memorising a bunch of text, it's in balancing whose activations you get to make all spicy.

As for gameplay itself, you have two objectives. Collect Wisps, the adorable little forest friends, and kill people. Do those things, and you score. The game goes for six rounds, with up to five activations per side, and speeds up fast as models die. Experienced wargamers will see the typical pattern of round 1 setup and jockeying for position, big action on rounds 2 and 3, then rounds 4 through 6 are fast paced and bloody as Fate currency access ramps up and the big cards start being played. High damage takes investment, but the health totals are in the sweet spot of not being paper thin (even the elves), and not being walking tanks (even the dwarfs).

Trust me, though, games can swing hard. Victory is determined at the end of the turn, and I've seen things flip from one person being on track to win to the other multiple times before a turn ends. There's a careful balance to strike of conservatism and aggression, particularly because you can - and will - lose points as well as gain them. You're seldom fully shut out of a game. 

Play time length, as a result, is pretty quick. After two weeks of playing, I was able to set up and finish inside of an hour and change, and that was including deckbuilding on the spot (generally, you'd come in with a prepared deck). Setting aside two hours for a game would allow plenty of time for social and chill, while potentially enabling a rematch if you fancied it. The fastest game I've ever played was about 40 minutes all told, and went to turn 4, so even rapid back-and-forth still gives you plenty of opportunities to do cool stuff.

If I'm making it sound all sunshine and rainbows, it's because it kind of... is. This is just a good game. It scratches the skirmish game itch for me perfectly, and I intend to play it a lot. That said, I have my unbiased reviewer hat on, so I want to point out a couple of issues.

Two of the Omen cards (out of 20 currently) have the potential to gotcha someone with an early game negative status effect, such as a model being locked in place or made to take minor damage over time. Nothing world ending, and the kind of thing you can trivially avoid if you know it's a possibility (basically, you just don't stand on the edge of deployment in a couple places), but I can see some people grumbling about it if they get got in their first game. I can see this changing before release, as the devs are sharpening things daily, so don't count on this being true even at the time of publication - I'm just obliged to review based on the rules as they exist right now.

The second is that, on release, every faction is model-locked. You need five in a list, everyone has five. So, while the deckbuilding is endlessly replayable, if you play a whole lot, you might want to see some new faces from time to time. That said, this is a temporary problem. By the time the Kickstarter ships, we're expecting one or two extra releases for each faction, which should vary things up. Again, though, I can't comment on what I haven't seen.

Final Thoughts

Emma: I've played a lot of wargames, and this one is easily one of my favourites. Definitely my favourite in the skirmish-level space. From what I understand of the Kickstarter, all the models are already with the factory, and they're just assessing demand levels, so the risk involved is low. I tried to decide what was my favourite part of the rules while writing this, and the number of options I wanted to put forward is a good sign. I tried asking the community, and everyone had something different to raise. So, I'll pick something minor and funny.

Witherwood Legions (the zombie fungus tree faction) has a leader that's just a giant, immobile tree that spawns tree tentacles. Its name is Yewen. Makes me laugh every time.

title: Detachment Focus: Berzerker Warband (Updated October 9, 2026)
content:
In this series of articles we take a deep dive into a specific Detachment for a faction, covering the faction’s rules and upgrades and talking about how to build around that faction for competitive play. In this article, we’re covering the Berzerker Warband Detachment for World Eaters.

The "main" Detachment for the World Eaters is the Berzerker Warband, an oft-updated version of their tenth edition Index Detachment. In many ways it's their most basic offering, giving a strong, persistent boost to the army and a number of solid stratagems, though these are primarily focused on buffing Berzerkers.

Changelog

  • 10-09-2026 (Latest): Updated for 11th Edition and the September Balance Dataslate
  • 4-26-2025: Updated for the 10th edition Codex
  • 6-1-2024: Initial Publication

Detachment Cost: 2 DP

Disposition: Purge the Foe

The Berzerker Warband is all about running Berzerkers. While there are a lot of rules in this Detachment which benefit other units, two key Stratagems - Apoplectic Frenzy and Berzerker’s Wrath - can only be used on Berzerker units. And given one of those lets you Advance and Charge, this is the best place to run your a 20-man unit of Berzerkers led by a Lord on Juggernaut. Otherwise, there are some solid utility pieces here, some powerful effects, and enough value for other units that this Detachment works well as a combined arms Detachment for World Eaters. The +1 Attack bonus is just generically good all the time.

The cost of this Detachment dropped from 3 DP to 2 DP in the September balance update, making it much better as an option and justifying the change in Detachment rule.

Detachment Rule: Relentless Rage

Friendly WORLD EATERS units' melee attacks have +1 A.

This used to be +2S and +1A on the charge, but was changed in the September Dataslate to just be +1 Attack all the time. That's about the same for Berzerkers, who went to S5 on their chainaxes and now have +1 Strength on the charge, and a little worse for everyone else - you no longer get S10 Power Fists with Terminators, for example. The upside to the change was the Detachment's DP cost dropped, letting you combine this with powerful effects in other Detachments, such as Wrath of Khorne in Vessels of Wrath.

Despite the loss of a Strength bonus on the charge, this is still a powerful army-wide rule to have, just making every unit you're fielding between 20% and 50% more effective in melee. It's still plenty good on Terminators, but generally speaking this rule is better the fewer attacks you started with. You especially want it for your Khornate Eviscerators, as those only get 3 Attacks, and will still hit at S9 on the charge.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Enhancements

The four Enhancements here are pretty solid, and can go on any Character.

  • Berzerker Glaive – The bearer gets +1 Attacks and +1 Damage for their melee weapons, excluding Extra Attacks weapons. This goes just fine on a Master of Executions but looks great on a Daemon Prince, where the combination of D4 Dev wounds and 10 attacks can do a lot of damage.
  • Helm of Brazen Ire – Reduces the damage characteristic of incoming attacks by 1. This is fine. It's best suited to a Daemon Prince, where the high toughness and wound counts give it the most mileage. If you really need to put it on a Lord o Juggernaut, that's fine too.
  • Favoured of Khorne – Each time you make a Blessings of Khorne roll, you can re-roll up to two of the dice as long as the bearer is on the battlefield. With fewer easy ways to re-roll dice in the Codex this is still an important ability… but not crucial unless you desperately need to get Angron back.
  • Battle-Lust – You can re-roll Charge rolls for the bearer’s unit, and if the Unbridled Bloodlust Blessing of Khorne is active, you get +1 to Charge rolls as well. This is a useful one for your key game plan of getting guys into melee, and note that it is all Charge rolls, so if you choose to make a Heroic Intervention you have a little less chance of an embarrassing failure there as well.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Stratagems

There are some solid Stratagems in this Detachment, and only two of them are locked to Berzerkers. Frenzied Resilience is the only 2 CP Stratagem in the bunch but they’re all pretty solid.

  • Blood Offering (Epic Deed, 1 CP) – Use in any phase on a WORLD EATERS unit from your army that was just destroyed while it was within range of one or more objective markers that you controlled at the end of the previous phase. Pick one of those objective markers to stay under your control until your opponent controls it at the end of a phase. This is great for forcing an opponent to come to you - use it for those times an opponent shoots you off an objective to sticky it and hold it, preserving your "Hold 1 outside your deployment zone" primary objective. The classic play here is to throw it on a solo lord on juggernaut, then park him on an objective as a durable holder and if an opponent kills him, boom - use this to sticky. These days I think you'd be better off with a unit which can use the HIDDEN rules.
  • Hack and Slash (Battle Tactic, 1 CP) – Use in the Fight phase on one WORLD EATERS unit that hasn’t fought yet and that made a Charge move this turn. Until the end of the phase, improve your AP by 1. A really useful Stratagem in an army where a lot of your common melee weapons are AP-1. Only getting +1 AP on the charge means this won’t be useful all the time (it won’t be triggered by a blood surge), but remember that it works after Heroic Intervention.
  • Frenzied Resilience (Battle Tactic, 2 CP) – Use in the Fight phase, just after an enemy unit has selected its targets. One WORLD EATERS unit targeted by those attacks gets -1 Damage. Identical to the Index version except for the name, and just as good - while also being potentially easier to pull off as your foot Daemon Princes can now make it cheaper. That’s huge if you plan on going into something like a unit of Bladeguard with a Justiciar to give them Fights First. Dropping this against Power fists or some other 2-damage threat to turn 10 dead Berzerkers into 5 is massive. It's also huge on a unit of Terminators, and that's something you might actually do now that you can combine this Detachment with Butchers of Khorne.
  • Skulls for the Skull Throne! (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Fight phase, just after a WORLD EATERS unit from your army destroys a CHARACTER or MONSTER model. Make a Blessings of Khorne roll and activate one Blessing of Khorne to be active until the end of the battle round in addition to your existing ones. Helpful, but be aware that you can’t use this to resurrect Angron any more, as his Reborn in Blood ability only works at the start of the battle round. This is fine, and what you really want this for most of the time is to activate 6” Consolidate moves. It can also be helpful if you’re going second and can pop this in your opponent’s turn.
  • Apoplectic Frenzy (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Use in your Movement phase, just after a Khorne Berzerkers unit is selected to Advance. That unit can Advance and charge. This is super important now that you don’t have access to this through the Blessings of Khorne, and one of the only ways to advance and charge in the army. Paired with 10” movement on Berzerkers led by a Lord on Juggernaut, this is how you get those nasty turn 1 charges.
  • Berzerker’s Wrath (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Use in your opponent’s Shooting phase when a Khorne Berzerkers unit would make a Blood Surge move as a result of those attacks. Instead of rolling a D6, your unit can automatically move up to 8”. A smart opponent will be playing around Blood Surge, but being able to get a guaranteed 8” off will make that a lot harder to do. This essentially makes it impossible for them to keep you out of range while being on an objective with you.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Playing This Detachment

If there’s one Detachment where you want to take the 20-model unit of Berzerkers, it’s this one. If you're doing that, the recipe here is easy: 20 Berzerkers with four Khornate Eviscerators, led by a Lord on Juggernaut. They move 10”, through walls, with the ability to Advance and Charge. You’ll want to keep a Daemon Prince nearby to pop Stratagems like Frenzied Resilience and Hack and Slash on them.

Now, with that said: Do you actually want to run one of these? Or two? That’s a tougher question. You definitely want to build around Berzerkers in this Detachment, but some of those will naturally want to be in Transports. Most of the time you're going to find it more convenient to run two or three 10-man units, led by Kharn and a Master of Executions with the Berzerker Glaive.  The Master of Executions is quite the beast he used to be, but he’s much cheaper now and worth adding to your Berzerker units for the ability to re-roll blood surges and to just get another model with a 2-damage attack in the unit. Kharn's a great way to get re-rolls and I’d strongly consider looking at a single unit of 3 Eightbound for their +1 to hit and wound aura.

Because the +1 Attacks benefit works on everything in your army, it’s worth pointint out that a ton of other units - Daemon Princes and melee vehicles like the Helbrute and Maulerfiend - really benefit from this upgrade, and can do their best work here. That makes the Berzerker Warband your best combined arms Detachment, even if you get some niftier buffs from the Goretrack Onslaught. [LANCE] after disembarking won’t do anything for a Defiler. The benefit is also great on Jakhals, who need the extra boost to be legitimate threats - and having them at S5 is a huge improvement that lets them punch way up.

When building lists with Berzerker Warband there are really two options to consider for your second Detachment:

  • Vessels of Wrath. This version gives you better Characters, and you'll likely want to take a third unit of Berzerkers led by a Master of Executions or a Lord on Juggernaut, maxing out on your Character counts for the army - that extra AP is huge, especially when stacked with the Hack and Slash Stratagem - going to AP-4 is a big deal for your units.
  • Butchers of Khorne. Terminators love getting +1 Attack and -1 Damage from the Frenzied Resilience Stratagem. They also love having +1 OC or +1 WS from the Enhancements in Butchers of Khorne, and getting an extra +1A from Focused Ferocity or +1 to Wound from A Trophy for the Throne. If you're going Terminator-heavy, this is your pick.

Strengths

  • Advance and Charge. This is the only place you’ll find it, and only on Berzerkers. But it’s still huge.
  • Melee buffs. That +1 Attack is a solid buff, and something that every fighty unit in your army wants. Even Land Raiders suddenly look scary with 10 attacks hitting on a 3+ and lethal/sustained hits.
  • DP Cost. At only 2 Detachment Points, this one's a steal. It's also a good way to get Purge the Foe as your Disposition, if you want it. The +1 Attack combos well with everything.

Weaknesses

  • Berzerker-focused. A couple of key Stratagems here only work on Berzerkers. And that’s a problem because…
  • Berzerkers. As a unit, berzerkers are kind of underwhelming. Imagine Assault Intercessors if they didn’t have re-rolls to wound. Yeah. They can do damage in volume, but you need stacked buffs to make them work. And they die quickly. 

Final Thoughts

The Berzerker Warband offers an exciting and balanced way to play World Eaters. Thanks to the September balance update, it's also the best way to play the army, combining in solid ways with the army's other Detachment options to buff key units across the army.

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. The Traveler’s Handbook introduces eight origins, four classes with two subclasses each, and six powerful Traveler Dynasties that serve as in-game factions. The Exodus Encyclopedia packs in stat blocks for constructs, Celestials, changelings, awakened beings, and human NPCs, along with Remnant items for research and combat.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

title: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana Returns – Chaosium’s Definitive Mythos Guide Hits in October
content:
Chaosium is releasing a new fourth edition of The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana this October, bringing the definitive guide to Lovecraftian horror back to shelves in full-color hardback format.

First published in 1994 and updated several times since, the book compiles detailed entries on mythos deities, creatures, tomes, and artifacts—from Azathoth to Zylac—tracing their appearances across fiction and pop culture. This new edition features updated text, evocative interior art, and a cover by John Sumrow, along with a fresh essay from author Dan Harms on the question “What is the Cthulhu Mythos?” Timelines of the Necronomicon, a cosmic horror bibliography, and illustrations of Nyarlathotep, Hastur, and Cthulhu himself round out the package.

The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana releases October 28—just in time to send a shiver down your spine before Halloween.

title: CMON Faces Make-or-Break Moment as It Warns of “Prolonged Structural Downturn”
content:
CMON has issued a stark warning about its future, telling investors its core business is stuck in a “prolonged structural downturn” and still burning through more cash than it brings in. The tabletop crowdfunding giant is now racing to raise up to $17.5m from outside investors.

The warning landed alongside CMON’s H1 financial report, and it caps off a brutal 18 months for one of the biggest names in crowdfunded board games.

Parts of this article is based on info from BoardGameWire.

A Company Half Its Former Size

CMON has spent the past year and a half trying to stop the bleeding. The publisher has:

  • Cut its workforce in half
  • Sold off major IP including Zombicide, Blood Rage, and Cthulhu: Death May Die
  • Shut down its Singapore office
  • Halted new crowdfunding campaigns

Those moves have helped — but not enough to fix the underlying problem.

Losses Shrinking, But Cash Still Draining

The good news: CMON’s losses are shrinking fast.

The company posted a loss of just over $2m in the first half of 2026, compared to nearly $7m during the same stretch last year. Revenue also crept up more than 7% year-on-year, hitting $3.68m. Selling and distribution costs were cut by more than half, and administrative expenses dropped from $4.37m to $2.37m.

The bad news: it’s still not enough to keep the lights on without outside help.

CMON’s cash reserves have been in freefall. They sat at $3.9m at the end of 2022, fell to $2.1m by the end of 2024, and slipped to just over $900,000 by June 2025. In early August, the company revealed it had roughly $368,000 on hand — less than a month’s worth of operating expenses.

The Backer Problem: $14m in Undelivered Games

A huge chunk of CMON’s financial pressure comes down to games that backers have already paid for but haven’t received.

Eight crowdfunded titles remain undelivered, representing $14m raised from backers. The two biggest are **DC Super Heroes United** (over $4.4m raised) and DCeased (over $2.5m). Both were originally due last year, but have been delayed repeatedly and are now slated for Q1 2027.

CMON hasn’t completed fulfillment on a crowdfunding project since Zombicide: White Death in mid-2025. It has managed to ship some pre-orders — Cthulhu: Dark Providence, Marvel United: Witching Hour, and Dune: Desert War all went out in the first half of this year — but four more pre-order titles remain in limbo, including the Assassin’s Creed Role Playing Game.

The $17.5m Gamble

To stay afloat, CMON is leaning on a massive rights issue designed to raise up to HK$150.5m (about $19m). The plan lets existing shareholders buy three new shares for every one they already own.

There’s just one problem: shareholders barely took the bait. Only 7.76% of the new shares were claimed by the August deadline, leaving CMON scrambling to find more than $17.5m from other investors — a figure approaching 2.5-times the company’s entire valuation from its last share sale in February.

If the money comes through, here’s how CMON plans to spend it:

  • 40% — Day-to-day operations for roughly a year, including staff, royalties, shipping, and distribution
  • 20% — Paying down debts, including $2.46m owed to a company director and $385,000 in unsecured employee advances
  • 25% — Expansion into existing and new markets, with a focus on Europe, Japan, and the Philippines
  • 15% — Potential acquisitions in digital gaming

The final result of the rights issue is due September 15.

A Digital Pivot — With a Catch

That 15% digital acquisition budget is notable, especially since CMON just walked away from a planned $2.1m investment in NFT game maker Blissful Link. That deal would have valued Blissful Link at over $95m — despite the company posting a loss of about $197,000 in 2024 on revenues of just over $408,000.

CMON says it’s now hunting for one to three businesses, mostly in Asia-Pacific, valued between $1.3m and $2.5m each, to help build digital adaptations and companion apps. The publisher insists physical tabletop games remain its core business and that digital is meant to complement, not replace, them.

Where the Money Comes From Now

The report also lays bare just how dramatically CMON’s geographic revenue has shifted.

North America generated over $8.6m in the first half of 2021 — 57% of the company’s roughly $15.1m revenue at the time. By the first half of 2026, North and South America combined brought in just $642,000.

Europe has collapsed similarly, falling from about $4.5m to $982,000 over the same period.

Asia is now CMON’s largest market by a wide margin, generating over $2m and accounting for about 55% of total revenue — up from less than 10% in 2021. That’s not because Asia is growing, though. Revenue there is down roughly 37% since 2022. It’s just fallen far less than everywhere else.

What’s Next for Crowdfunding?

CMON said back in March that it intended to resume crowdfunding in the second half of 2026. Its latest report doesn’t repeat that promise. Instead, the company says new titles will be developed and launched “selectively” based on market conditions, available cash, and project readiness.

For a publisher built on the crowdfunding model, that’s a notable shift in tone — and a sign that CMON’s road back to stability is still a long one.

title: This Monty Python-esque comedy RPG lets you improv as a band of incompetent and dangerously powerful wizards
content:
Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is a new tabletop roleplaying game that allows players to become powerful and incompetent spellcasters.

The upcoming roleplaying game sees any number of players collaborating together to tell a story about a band of chaotic wizards. Similarly to the likes of absurdist, fantastical comedy such as the works of iconic British group Monty Python, alongside the likes of The Mighty Boosh and What We Do in the Shadows, Hello Wizard I have a Problem is all about rapid scenes infused by the strange and unexpected.

Unlike many other tabletop RPGs, Hello Wizard sees its players taking turns to take on the roles of player character and games master. Each scene in Hello Wizard has a single player take the spotlight as their spellcaster, with the goal of impressing their fellow sorcerers with their magic. The active player describes what spells their wizard casts, with the other players acting collectively as a GM and deciding how these spells can go wrong.

Players will use a Problem Generator included in the fantasy RPG’s rulebook as inspiration for what could go wrong with the wizards’ spells, with the book capable of making over “200,000” prompts for possible disastrous outcomes. Once every player has had the opportunity to step into the spellcasting spotlight at least a few times, the game ends and players tally up their ‘points’ - which are decided by a loose improv system - and determine who is the most impressive wizard.

The rules system for Hello Wizard is very straightforward and intended to be easy for players to learn. Setup for the tabletop RPG is also designed to be quick and easy, with players expected to start in little time. The rulebook for the game will contain advice and optional rules players can use to augment their playthroughs too.

Hello Wizard I have a Problem was created by Sam Armstrong, a tabletop RPG designer who has previously made titles such as All Bastard - a fantasy TRPG in which players take the roles of either a band of bragging heroes or the bastards they defeated - and horror roleplaying game Slasher. The artwork for the game was created by illustrator Evlyn Moreau, who has previously worked on RPGs like Liminal High School.

The crowdfunding campaign for Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is on Kickstarter until later this afternoon, with the title potentially being made available on Armstrong’s Itch.io page. A pledge of £8 ($10) will get backers a physical copy of the game in June, alternatively a PDF version is available for £4 ($5).

title: Re-enact Greta Gerwig’s Little Women with this coming-of-age tabletop RPG
content:
New tabletop roleplaying game, Castles in the Air, will enable players to re-enact their favourite coming-of-age stories.

Castles in the Air was inspired by the likes of classic coming-of-age period dramas such as Little Women by Louisa May Alcott - which was adapted into a 2019 film directed by Greta Gerwig and starring Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Florence Pugh, Laura Dern and Timothee Chalamet - and Anne of Green Gables by Lucy Maud Montgomery, which was adapted into a televisions series in 2017 by Netflix.

The upcoming roleplaying game will see players’ characters grow up together from children to adults during the historical era known as the Gilded Age, which took place in the USA from the 1870s to the 1890s and saw an increase in industrialisation, economic growth and migration to the US. Castles in the Air is a collaborative storytelling game in which players construct narratives that centre around the wonders and fears of childhood, before tackling the joys and hardships of adulthood.

Players begin the tabletop RPG as a tight-knit group of children, all of whom have great expectations of their futures and much quieter current lives. In this phase of the story, players develop a shared childhood together by doing the things rural and financially supported kids did during that era: like playing in their local farmlands, swimming in the lakes and watching the stars.

As the player characters grow up, they’ll begin exploring other feelings and ideas that come with age. Characters in the group might develop a crush on someone or form a heated rivalry with one of the other local children. All the while, the player group will grow up together, before eventually reaching adulthood and potentially finding themselves drifting apart as life takes them in different directions - perhaps to only meet once again.

Players will be able to create their characters in Castles in the Air by choosing from a variety of character roles inspired by classic archetypes, such as the troublesome scamp, studious bookworm or spoiled princess. Add onto this a dream, childhood relationships, a family background and a bosom enemy, and players can even create their favourite characters from the likes of Little Women or Anne of Green Gables.

Castles in the Air was designed and written by Melia Carraway, with contributions from co-created by the co-founders of the RPG’s publisher, Storybrewer’s Roleplaying, Vee Hendro and Hayley Gordon, who also co-designed Good Society: a tabletop RPG inspired by the works of Jane Austen.

The crowdfunding campaign for Castles in the Air is on Kickstarter until June 9th, with a pledge of AU$ 99 (£52/$77) getting backers a physical copy of the game in March 2025. Alternatively, players can get a digital version for a pledge of AU$ 34 (£18/$26).

title: Freak War throws Exploding Kittens and Pokémon into a blender for a trading card game you can play at parties
content:
Take the evolving monsters of Pokémon, cross them with the fast-playing chaos of party game hit Exploding Kittens and you end up with something that looks a lot like Freak War, a new party-game TCG that wants to offer the fun battles of trading card games without the effort of learning lots of rules or building a deck.

Freak War is the creation of Nate Galbraith, aka cartoonist sketchnate, who was inspired after watching kids trying to have Pokémon battles using Uno cards, before suggesting they play classic playing card game War (which you might also know as Battle) instead. The result was a mixture of all three, with Galbraith adding a collection of strange creatures to the cards.

Unlike the head-to-head battles of Pokémon, Freak War can be played with up to four (or more) players, who can simply split the shuffled deck between them to play - though there is the option to build your own custom decks if you really want to.

Everyone plays a creature at the same time, with the highest attack level winning the battle. Like Exploding Kittens, the many cards can also introduce various effects that shake things up, including the power to evolve into bigger creatures - Pokémon-style - and equip modifiers to your own or opponent’s cards to boost or reduce their strength.

Whether the players choose a card from their hand or simply flip the top of their deck depends on the mode they’re playing: the more chaotic War, or the more strategic Battle. Both modes can be modified further by King of the Hill and team rules.

If two players draw in attack level, they both discard a card before facing off by playing another creature. The overall winner takes all the cards played and adds them to their win pile, which are reshuffled into the player’s deck - the person who manages to claim all the cards from their opponents, wins.

The weird and wonderful creatures on the cards have a bit of lore behind them, having been created by the emergence of a second sun that mutated familiar animals like rabbits, foxes and fish into muscly fishpeople, a time-travelling tiger, a partying platypus, a dog with a goldfish bowl for a head, a sad bee and a Man Cat that appears to basically be a bloke in a cat costume, among others.

Modifier cards, meanwhile, range from a Super Sword (and a Super Duper Sword) to the power to swap cards with a rival, cancel a modifier or flip coins for the chance of a power boost. Some of the creature effects get playfully meta in the way you’d expect for a party game too, with the scrap-loving Fly Guy gaining power if there’s uneaten food near the players.

As someone who is admittedly tired of many copy-paste or just downright gross party games (looking at you, double-offending Cards Against Humanity clones), I’m fairly charmed by Galbraith’s goofy creations and the sprinkling of chaotic take-that gameplay in the form of a TCG. (The card layout is quite explicitly inspired by Pokémon cards.) Sure, it’s not going to be for everyone, but as something knowingly silly to fill five minutes with friends and family (especially younger players), it looks like solid, breezy fun for $20 a deck. With a bunch of different packs filled with dozens more creatures from buff penguins to cute-looking snails, I’m pretty intrigued just to see Galbraith’s interpretation of the nonsense of modern Pokémon evolutions, too.

Freak War has already passed its fairly modest crowdfunding goal of $10,000 over on Kickstarter, where its campaign will run until June 13th. The game itself is expected to land with backers next June, just in time to take on holiday.
